items.summary: Network design problems form a classic subfield of online algorithms, but almost nothing is known about their more challenging vertex-connectivity variants. We initiate the study of online vertex-connectivity network design for arbitrary demand pairs by considering the fundamental problem of connectivity augmentation. In an instance of \emph{Online Vertex Connectivity Augmentation} (OVCA), we are given a $k$-vertex-connected graph $F$ and a set of additional purchasable edges (with costs). Demand pairs $(s_1,t_1),(s_2,t_2),\dots$ then arrive online. Upon each arrival, the algorithm must irrevocably purchase edges so that $s_i$ and $t_i$ become $(k{+}1)$-vertex-connected in the union of $F$ with all edges purchased so far. Our main contribution is an $O((k+\log n)\log n)$-competitive online algorithm for OVCA. We also give an offline $O(k+\log n)$-approximation algorithm. We obtain our algorithms via a structural dichotomy on the minimum vertex cuts of $F$. We note that some dependence on $k$ in the approximation ratio is necessary -- i.e., the problem is hard to approximate within any $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factor independent of $k$ -- which shows a separation from the edge-connectivity setting. Finally, specializing to $k=1$, our methods yield the first polylogarithmic-competitive online algorithm for a vertex-connectivity survivable network design problem, namely an $\widetilde O(\log^3 n)$-competitive algorithm for online $\{1,2\}$-VC-SNDP (i.e., an SNDP variant where each demand pair comes with a vertex-connectivity requirement of $1$ or $2$).

items.title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
items.summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.

items.title: An Empirical Square-Root Law for the Degree Discrepancy of Binary m-Sequences
items.summary: Let $k\ge 2$, $N=2^k$, $M=N-1$ and let $Δ(r)$ be the range, over all starting offsets, of the total-variation degree discrepancy of a length-$r$ window of a primitive binary linear feedback shift register (LFSR) of period $M$. Degree-discrepancy profiles for every $k\le 28$ support the scaling $\max_r Δ(r)=Θ(\sqrt{N})=Θ(2^{k/2})$. The tabulated peaks are maxima on a discrete grid, hence lower bounds on the exhaustive maximum. The normalized peaks $d_k=\max_{r\in R_k}Δ(r)/2^{k/2}$ oscillate between values near 1/2 and values that approach, but do not exceed, 1. The data suggest $\liminf d_k=1/2$ and $\limsup d_k\le 1$. We conjecture the same square-root law for the exhaustive maximum, with those normalized envelopes. A Brownian-bridge heuristic accounts for the square-root scale. The same profiles do not place the recorded maximizer at mid-path: after folding by the complement identity $Δ(M-r)=Δ(r)$, the median of $\min(ρ^*_k,1-ρ^*_k)$ is 0.35, and several $k$ (notably 16 and 28) peak on a short window. Mid-horizon $Δ$ remains a large fraction of the peak, so the square-root scale can still come from a Brownian-bridge envelope. The same range has two readings of the starting offset: a pairing fragment in serial-knockout scheduling, and a change to the plaintext on an LFSR orbit. The location of the maximizer is not part of the conjecture. Open questions that separate the conjecture from a theorem are listed.

items.title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
items.summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

items.title: A Parallel Greedy Algorithm for Maximal b-Matching in Hypergraphs
items.summary: We present \parallelBatchBMatch, a parallel batch-vote algorithm for maximal $b$-matching in hypergraphs. The algorithm is deterministic for a given ordering of edges and produces the same output as the sequential greedy algorithm, i.e., the lexicographically first maximal $b$-matching. Under a uniformly random priority order it performs $O(m')$ expected work in the binary fork--join model, where $m'$ is the number of pins, the total number of vertex--edge incidences. The algorithm performs at most $m$ rounds for every priority order, where $m$ is the number of edges. Every round of the algorithm has $O(\log^2 m')$ depth with high probability, and thus the total depth of the algorithm is $O(m \log^2 m')$ with high probability. We implement the parallel algorithm in CUDA and evaluate it on real-world hypergraphs with capacities $b \in \{1, 3, 5\}$. The parallel algorithm computes the same matchings as the greedy algorithms and for the case of $b = 5$ it is up to $19.07$ times faster than the existing state-of-the art greedy algorithm.

items.title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
items.summary: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.

items.title: Rateless Coding for Efficient Model Broadcast in Federated Learning
items.summary: Model broadcast in federated learning (FL) with wireless channels faces significant challenges due to large model sizes and heterogeneous, unreliable channel conditions. While rateless coding has been widely adopted in modern broadcast communications to handle channel heterogeneity, its potential for model broadcast in FL remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we propose a joint source-channel coding scheme based on rateless coding to improve the robustness and efficiency of downlink model broadcast in FL. Specifically, we establish a rigorous convergence analysis of FL to inform the rateless code and quantization design under noisy downlink channel conditions. Moreover, by observing that the iterative process of FL naturally provides prior information about client updates, we leverage client-side local models as conditional prior information to aid the decoding process, thereby reducing transmission costs. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our rateless coding scheme significantly enhances downlink model broadcast efficiency in FL, while retaining comparable training accuracies for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions.

items.title: A Rigorous Fredholm Framework and Stabilized Equal-Order Finite Element Methods for the Time-Harmonic Biot Model
items.summary: We investigate the well-posedness and finite element approximation of a three-field formulation of the time-harmonic Biot model, motivated by frequency-domain magnetic resonance elastography. The underlying complex-valued mixed variational problem is noncoercive because of the inertial elasticity term and the coupled three-field structure. Continuous well-posedness is established under a non-resonance condition by decomposing the variational operator into an invertible principal part and a compact perturbation and applying the Fredholm alternative. We then develop stabilized equal-order finite element methods based on momentum-residual stabilization and local projection stabilization of the pore pressure. For the discrete problem, we establish mesh-uniform stability and well-posedness on sufficiently fine meshes via an a priori stability estimate and a Schatz-type compactness argument, without invoking discrete $T$-coercivity. Optimal-order a priori error estimates are derived in the natural energy norm. We also develop systematic selection principles for the stabilization parameters. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates and demonstrate stable approximations for heterogeneous low-permeability media and anatomically realistic brain geometries relevant to magnetic resonance elastography.

items.title: Probabilistically Exact Convexification of Mixed-Integer Quadratic Optimization with Indicators
items.summary: We study the convexification of mixed-integer quadratic optimization with indicator variables. The problem remains NP-hard even when the quadratic matrix has bandwidth two, posing a fundamental obstacle to tractable exact convexification. To overcome this challenge in realistic settings, we introduce probabilistically exact (inner) convexification, a framework that relaxes the requirement of exactness for every objective while preserving exact optimality for statistically relevant ones. Our approach is motivated by inference applications, where the objective is determined by a data vector drawn from a distribution and a regularization vector chosen from a prescribed family. Our convexification preserves the exactness of the optimal value with high probability over the data distribution, simultaneously for every regularization vector in this family. We apply this notion to quadratic matrices of any fixed bandwidth. Despite their worst-case NP-hardness, we construct probabilistically exact convexifications that admit exact extended second-order cone formulations of size polynomial in the dimension $n$ and the inverse failure probability $1/δ$. The required assumptions for their high-probability exactness are surprisingly mild: they accommodate both light-tailed and heavy-tailed data, including distributions without finite mean, as well as arbitrary nonnegative regularization coefficients.

items.title: Markov Population Potential Game: An Alternative Framework for Markovian Traffic Assignment
items.summary: Understanding the equilibrium behavior of large populations of interacting agents in transportation systems is challenging due to the high-dimensional state space and the coupled decision-making among agents. This study proposes the Markov population potential game (MPPG) that integrates Markov games, potential games, and population games as a unified framework for analyzing such interactions. The framework extends the classical Markov potential game to the population level and establishes theoretical conditions on stage rewards and state transitions under which the Markov population game admits a Beckmann-type potential function. Accordingly, every KKT point of the associated optimization problem yields an MPPG equilibrium. We further demonstrate that if only the reward condition holds, each KKT point of the optimization problem corresponds to a support-restricted $\varepsilon$-equilibrium, meaning the Q-values of any two active actions differ by at most $\varepsilon$, thereby significantly extending the applicability of MPPG. We further establish both priori and posteriori upper bounds of $\varepsilon$ to efficiently evaluate the approximation error. Inspired by the equivalent optimization problem, a projected-gradient (PG) policy iteration algorithm is developed. The theoretical bounds and PG algorithm are demonstrated through numerical experiments on a parametric Markov population game.

items.title: Finite Element Approximation of Three-Dimensional Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Curve-Supported Controls
items.summary: We consider a linear-quadratic elliptic optimal control problem in three dimensions with a box-constrained control supported on a compact embedded $C^{1,1}$ curve strictly contained in a bounded convex polyhedral domain. The right-hand side of the state equation is a measure supported on the curve, and the state is singular along it. We establish well-posedness and first-order optimality conditions and derive curve-adapted weighted inequalities and finite element error estimates for the singular state. For continuous piecewise linear finite elements on quasi-uniform tetrahedral meshes and variational discretization of the control, assuming exact integration over the curve, we prove the almost quadratic estimate $\|\bar q-\bar q_h\|_{L^2(γ)}\le Ch^2(1+\abs{\ln h})^3$. The proof of this estimate requires new results, which are of independent interest. The convergence rate observed in a numerical experiment is consistent with the predicted algebraic order.

items.title: Subadditivity and the failure of strong subadditivity in the Nichols--Wootters family of entropies
items.summary: We prove subadditivity for the Nichols--Wootters family of entropies interpolating between the von Neumann entropy and the subentropy, with all spectra evaluated in one common ambient dimension. Beyond the von Neumann entropy, equality holds exactly when at least one marginal is pure. This settles the subadditivity conjecture concerning subentropy. Every member except the von Neumann entropy fails strong subadditivity, already on a maximally entangled two-qubit state tensored with a mixed qubit. Its strong-subadditivity defect takes both signs on quantum Markov states. For a pure bipartite state tensored with an ancillary state, we identify the defect with a separately concave product gap and determine its exact maximum under rank constraints. For arbitrary bipartite states, we obtain an explicit lower bound in the marginal purities. For two-qubit states, we determine the optimal coefficient multiplying the product of the smaller marginal eigenvalues in every common ambient dimension, including the subentropy coefficient $1/3$. A positive representation by Haar averages of compressed matrix entropies gives the pinching inequality underlying these results and also yields entropy-gain bounds for unital quantum channels.As an application, each entropy equals the classical communication capacity retained after a specified isotropic partial projective measurement, at a prescribed average input state, even when entangled block encodings are allowed.

items.title: A polynomial-time approximation scheme for the weighted Euclidean Minimum Latency Problem in fixed dimension
items.summary: In the Traveling Salesman Problem, a route must visit all customers and return to its starting point while minimizing its total length. The Minimum Latency Problem, also known as the Traveling Repairman Problem, instead minimizes the sum of the times at which customers are first visited. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the weighted Euclidean Minimum Latency Problem in every fixed dimension, with arbitrary nonnegative customer weights. Our proof restricts the form of a solution in three steps, each with a controlled increase in cost. First, a decomposition based on Sitters' method assigns customers to phases that start and end at the root. Second, within each phase, we divide the route into a constant number of blocks and charge each customer at the end of its assigned block. The resulting objective is a nonnegative linear combination of block lengths. Third, we add an auxiliary dimension and use a fixed Minkowski norm to close each block path into a tour. Arora's closed-tour estimate then gives paths that cross the boundaries of a common dissection only at designated portals and a bounded number of times per face. A dynamic program optimizes the restricted objective, and projecting its paths back to the original space gives the final route. Rounding weights and coordinates keeps the state space polynomial.

items.title: Wiener-path-based exact and splitting simulation of linear and semi-linear SDEs with additive noise
items.summary: Strong, or pathwise, simulation of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) requires linking a generated SDE path to the corresponding realization of its driving Wiener process. In this work, we develop Wiener-path-based simulation procedures for multidimensional linear and semi-linear SDEs with additive noise that preserve this connection. Building upon a known Wiener-path-based exact simulation approach for linear SDEs, we extend this construction to generate coherent paths simultaneously on different time grids. We further propose an alternative exact simulation procedure that requires fewer random numbers and therefore provides a more efficient construction, while retaining a controlled approximation of the coupling between the SDE path and its associated Wiener path. The proposed methods are illustrated on a stochastic harmonic oscillator, a well-known model from classical mechanics, with the simulation results confirming the theoretical findings. We then extend the Wiener-path-based construction to semi-linear SDEs, which arise in many real-world applications. In contrast to linear SDEs, their solutions are generally not available in closed form, making numerical approximation methods necessary. For Euler--Maruyama-type methods, the relation between a given Wiener path and the corresponding approximate SDE path is explicit, whereas constructing Wiener-path-based simulations using structure-preserving splitting methods is less immediate. We address this challenge by incorporating the aforementioned Wiener-path-based constructions into splitting methods. Illustrations on the stochastic FitzHugh--Nagumo model and the stochastic Jansen--Rit neural mass model, two important models from neuroscience, demonstrate the applicability of the proposed procedures to non-linear stochastic systems.

items.title: Integrality Gap of 3.4 for Santa Claus: A Topology-based Analysis
items.summary: In the \textsc{Max-Min Allocation} problem, a set of indivisible items are to be assigned to a set of players and the goal is to maximize the minimum value among all players. A much studied special case, the \textsc{Santa Claus} problem, assumes that an item has a fixed utility but a player is only interested in a subset of items. The main technique for designing approximation algorithms for \textsc{Santa Claus} is the configuration LP, introduced by the Bansal and Sviridenko. A long line of research has progressively improved the upper bound of the integrality gap, mostly relying on the combinatorial arguments of Haxell for finding perfect matchings in certain hypergraphs. Remarkably, a recent paper of Haxell and Szabó (SODA '23) introduced a novel topology-based analysis, by which they are able to obtain the current best upper bound of $3.534$. In this work, we adapt the approach of Haxell and Szabó to analyze the integrality gap. The main new ingredient in our adaptation is that we stop the process of "edge explosions" in a graph used by Haxell and Szabó when it becomes too costly. This early termination of explosions, combined with a new lower bound on a topological connectivity parameter based on a theorem of Aharoni, Berger, and Meshulam, allows us to improve the integrality gap to $3.4$. Our analysis has the additional advantage of being simpler.

items.title: Multimodal Semantic Communication using Shared and Unique Representation Decomposition
items.summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm for bandwidth-constrained mobile and vehicular networks. This paper proposes a unified representation learning framework for multimodal SemCom (MSC), which encodes heterogeneous data into a compact semantic space for efficient transmission and source recovery. The framework addresses the multimodal semantic representation gap, which arises when at least one modality contains semantic information that cannot be fully inferred from the other. To preserve this information for reconstruction, the framework decomposes each representation into shared and modality-specific components. We formulate a mutual information objective for source reconstruction, cross-modal alignment of the shared components, and decoupling of the shared and modality-specific components. To enhance transmission efficiency, we introduce a shared knowledge base implemented as a compact codebook of semantic vectors learned during training. The shared components are transmitted digitally as codebook indices, while the modality-specific components are sent in analog form. We apply knowledge distillation during training, using a pretrained vision foundation model to guide the learning of quantized shared features. On image--text pairs over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Extended Vehicular A (EVA) channels, the proposed framework improves image reconstruction over conventional separate source-channel coding (SSCC) and representative multimodal and unimodal SemCom systems. Further evaluations show gradual degradation under channel-estimation mismatch, complementary effects of alignment, decoupling, and knowledge distillation on the shared representation, and alignment of shared features across modalities with separation of the modality-specific features.

items.title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
items.summary: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.

items.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
items.summary: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

items.title: Numerical solution of the Cauchy problem for second-order evolutionary equations with damped sinusoidal memory
items.summary: We consider the Cauchy problem for a second-order evolutionary equation with an integral term containing the convolution of a memory kernel with the second derivative of the solution. The kernel is specified by a finite sum of damped sinusoidal functions with positive damping coefficients, amplitudes, and frequencies. A transformation of the original nonlocal problem into an equivalent local system of coupled second-order differential equations with additional variables is proposed. For the local system, an energy identity with a dissipative term is constructed and a priori estimates of the solution are obtained. On the basis of the local formulation, a three-level difference scheme with a weight parameter is considered. The decrease of the discrete energy under standard constraints on the weight parameter is proved, which ensures unconditional stability of the scheme in the corresponding energy norm. The theoretical consideration is supplemented by the results of numerical solution of a problem with memory for a one-dimensional wave equation.

items.title: Hyperexponential Stabilization of Nonholonomic Systems by Oscillating Controls
items.summary: We address the problem of designing time-varying feedback controls that stabilize a given equilibrium of a nonholonomic system at a faster than the exponential rate. We consider systems with an arbitrary degree of nonholonomy and prove a theorem on practical hyperexponential stabilization under a suitable assumption on the parameterized dither signals. The convergence proof is based on a comparison equation with a prescribed power of logarithmic terms. We apply this result to stabilize a model of a car with two off-hooked trailers.

items.title: Surface evolution under conformal map and linearized energy-stable parametric finite element methods
items.summary: In this paper, we aim to develop a linearized, energy-stable, second-order-in-time parametric finite element method without Lagrange multipliers for surface evolution equations on surfaces with or without boundaries, including (volume-preserving) mean curvature flow and surface diffusion. We first reformulate the original equations into a new unified form in which the tangential motion is determined by requiring the flow map to be conformal. Based on this new formulation, we present a family of parametric finite element schemes that employ a linearized Euler or Crank-Nicolson discretization in time. We prove the existence and uniqueness of the resulting linear system, as well as the energy stability of the schemes. Our discrete methods can be applied to general surfaces although the second-order scheme may degenerate to first-order accuracy in certain cases. Numerical results verify the robustness of our method and demonstrate its ability to preserve mesh quality.

items.title: Delaunay-Based Nearest Neighbor Search with Grid-Accelerated Queries and Parallel Construction
items.summary: Nearest-neighbor search is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, with applications in distance field computation, surface reconstruction, and point cloud registration. In many graphics applications, data points lie on a surface manifold embedded in 3D space, whereas queries are distributed throughout the surrounding volume, a setting in which spatial partitioning structures such as k-d trees and grids can become inefficient. Dynamic-programming-based nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) offers an alternative: it traverses a successor DAG that records the history of incremental Delaunay construction and often outperforms spatial partitioning structures. However, its sequential construction is slow, and naive parallelization degrades query performance, limiting its practical adoption. We accelerate both queries and construction in DP-NNS. For queries, we introduce a grid-based initialization strategy that precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG, shortening search paths while preserving exactness and enabling a twofold speedup. For construction, we analyze how parallel insertion affects query cost and develop a parallel algorithm that preserves logarithmic expected query cost under stated geometric assumptions. Our parallel construction algorithm achieves a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline while maintaining nearly the same query cost. We further reorder query points to improve cache locality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms widely used libraries in nearest-neighbor query performance.

items.title: Floating-point, exact and certified computation for control: paradigms, pitfalls, and how to combine them
items.summary: Many questions in linear systems theory have a discrete answer: is a polynomial Hurwitz, is a 2-D system structurally stable, is the peak gain finite, which solution of a Riccati equation is stabilizing? Algorithms implemented in floating point usually answer such questions, but often with a limited, or even no, guarantee on the result, which depends on a tolerance fixed a priori. Computer algebra and interval arithmetic provide other ways of computing, which give guarantees on the result, but usually at a higher cost. In this paper, we propose a short guide to these approaches: floating-point, exact, multiprecision and interval arithmetic, certified root isolation and certified Newton methods. Using small examples from control theory (each of them runs in a few seconds), we show what each approach guarantees and in which situations it fails, and how several approaches can be combined, for example by certifying a numerical solution, or by reducing a problem exactly before solving it with certified real solving. We then revisit the structural stability of 2-D systems (with and without parameters) and the computation of the $H_\infty$ norm, and we list the available implementations. The main examples are given as reproducible worksheets based on the PACE ecosystem.

items.title: Small classes have linear neighbourhood complexity
items.summary: A hereditary graph class is small if it contains at most $n!c^n$ labelled graphs on $n$ vertices for some constant $c$. Small classes include proper minor-closed classes and classes of bounded twin-width. We prove that every small class has linear neighbourhood complexity, that is, in every graph in the class, vertex neighbourhoods intersect any $k$-vertex set in only $O(k)$ distinct ways. This resolves a conjecture of Bonnet, Duron, and the first two authors (ITCS 2025) and makes the algorithmic, structural, and representation consequences of linear neighbourhood complexity available for every small class. In particular, every small class admits an adjacency labelling scheme with $O(\log^2 n)$-bit labels, improving the previous $O(\log^3 n)$ bound.

items.title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
items.summary: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

items.title: Multicontinuum Poroelasticity Model. Analysis and Computation
items.summary: In this work, we develop and analyze a macroscopic multicontinuum model for Biot poroelasticity. The full macroscopic multicontinuum system is derived by projecting the microscopic weak formulation onto continuum-dependent Galerkin spaces enriched with first-order multiscale corrections. This construction retains generalized pressure storage and coupling terms, with effective coefficients inherited from the microscopic bilinear forms. Under suitable coefficient assumptions, we establish well-posedness and energy stability of the macroscopic multicontinuum model. A fully discrete scheme combining the Galerkin finite element method in space with the backward Euler method in time is then developed. Its well-posedness and stability are proved, and a priori error estimates are derived using appropriate projection operators and energy arguments. Finally, numerical experiments for periodic and non-periodic high-contrast media demonstrate the accuracy of the multicontinuum model with respect to the averaged fine-scale solution.

items.title: Exact Decisions and Certified Values in $L_\infty$-Norm Computation from State-Space Representations
items.summary: Computing the $L_\infty$-norm of a time-invariant linear ordinary differential control system is a routine task in robust control, usually delegated to floating-point routines that perform well on most practical systems. Behind the numerical value, however, lies a discrete decision: whether a pole lies on the imaginary axis, and whether a mode of a realization is actually a pole of the transfer matrix. Floating-point arithmetic can only replace this decision with a tolerance. This paper explains, for a control audience, what reliable symbolic-numeric computation offers for this problem: exact arithmetic where a decision has to be made, and certified enclosures where a value has to be computed. We show how the problem is turned into a small polynomial system directly from state-space data, how this system is solved in practice, and what it costs. A benchmark on the {\tt COMPleib} library and on families of systems with known norms shows that two standard numerical routines err in opposite directions on the imaginary-axis decision, and never on the same system, while the certified method decides it correctly on every instance tested and computes the norm at a cost comparable to that of the numerical routines on most systems. We conclude with practical guidelines for users of numerical tools.

items.title: Higher order schemes for the numerical solution of integro-differential equation-based age-of-infection models with time-dependent contact rates
items.summary: Age-of-infection models, formulated as integro-differential equations (IDEs), provide elegant mathematical descriptions for the spread of infectious diseases. In contrast to ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based models, IDE-based models can accommodate general distributions of transition times between disease stages. Yet, the accurate numerical assessment of the solution of IDE models remains challenging. Here, we extend a recently proposed fixed-point method based on Gregory quadrature. We generalize the formulation to time-dependent contact rates whose changes at discrete time points are represented by continuously differentiable sigmoidal interpolants, and suggest additional finite difference approximations to obtain higher-order schemes for susceptible, infected and recovered subpopulations. The resulting numerical schemes achieve convergence orders of two, three and four for all three subpopulations, enabling accurate and flexible simulations of IDE-based epidemic models with general sojourn time distributions and changing contact patterns.

items.title: Higher order convergence rate in probability for approximations of the stochastic Burgers and Cahn-Hilliard equation
items.summary: We consider temporal approximations of stochastic PDEs driven by additive space-time white noise, with nonlinearities that may lose both integrability and regularity. Our key examples are the stochastic Burgers equation in dimension 1 and the stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation in dimensions $\leq 3$. We show that the accelerated exponential Euler scheme achieves a rate of convergence in probability that is well beyond the state of the art: arbitrarily close to $3/4$ in the case of Burgers and $1-d/8$ in the case of Cahn-Hilliard.

items.title: Fast Subproblem Solving in Benders Decomposition for Affine Potential-Based Flow Problems with Topology Switching and Scenarios
items.summary: Potential-based flow problems arise for a range of practical problems, like the operation of lossless power networks. The distribution of flows through the network is governed by the potential equation, which relates arc flows and node potentials following arc potential functions. We consider a general variant with affine potential functions, topology switching, and scenarios. It can be solved using a Benders decomposition algorithm, with each scenario corresponding to a subproblem. Subproblem solving time can then significantly contribute to overall running time. We present a fast algorithm to obtain Benders optimality and feasibility cuts from fixed master solutions. Problems with affine potential functions are reduced to equivalent problems where every potential function is the identity function. Optimal primal and dual solutions as well as unbounded dual rays are determined by systems of linear equations (SLE), resulting in a constant number of SLEs solved per subproblem. SLEs are solved using LU-factorizations, with the similarity between primal and dual, scenarios, and master solutions exploited by reusing factorizations via low-rank updates to significantly reduce theoretical complexity. We demonstrate the method on security-constrained optimal transmission switching instances, where subproblem solve time reductions of 97.98 percent compared to a standard LP solver are observed.

items.title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
items.summary: We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product. In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds. In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

items.title: Hybrid Precoding and Combining for O-RAN Massive MIMO Systems
items.summary: Recently, the radio access network (RAN) has been reimagined through open RAN (O-RAN) architecture to overcome the limitations of the traditional monolithic, black-box design philosophy and to leverage emerging technologies such as cloud computing, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. Although O-RAN disaggregates the base station (BS) into independent components to enable modular deployment, this paradigm introduces new challenges in signal processing and beamforming. In particular, beamforming in O-RAN must account for fronthaul link (FHL) capacity constraints, coordinated operation of multiple radio units (possibly from different vendors), and resource management, including transmit power allocation. To address these challenges, this work proposes novel beamforming techniques for a downlink multiuser hybrid massive multiple-input multiple-output system, in which hybrid architectures are deployed at both the users and at each BS radio unit. We formulate a sum-rate maximization problem incorporating transmit-power, unit-modulus, and FHL capacity constraints. The proposed algorithm integrates gradient descent and the Lagrange multiplier method to design analog beamformers and digital precoders, respectively, whereas digital combiners are designed to render the received streams parallel to each other. By avoiding computationally intensive operations such as eigenvalue and singular value decompositions, the proposed approach, as evidenced by simulation results, achieves superior performance with moderate computational complexity compared to existing benchmark schemes.

items.title: Robust High-Order BUG Integrators without Basis Augmentation
items.summary: We develop robust high-order basis-update and Galerkin (BUG) integrators for dynamical low-rank approximation without basis augmentation or rank truncation. The basis and core updates use the same approximate increment. We establish a two-sided relaxed-exactness estimate that controls the error in the low-rank approximation by the increment error. Under the stated assumptions on the vector field and its normal component, sufficiently accurate increments yield local and global error bounds whose constants and step-size restrictions are independent of small singular values. Using explicit Runge--Kutta increments, we obtain robust orders two, three, and four for the explicit midpoint method, Heun's third-order method, and Merson's fourth-order method, respectively. Every internal stage and final approximation has rank at most the prescribed rank $r$. We also prove that these orders are retained under arbitrary basis augmentation followed by best rank-$r$ SVD truncation at the internal stages and the endpoint, without a separate assumption on the truncation error. Numerical experiments confirm the convergence orders and show comparable performance with and without augmentation.

items.title: On Star Monotone Operators: Theory and Applications
items.summary: Introduced by Solodov and Svaiter \cite{SS}, star monotone operators have repeatedly appeared as a sufficient condition ensuring global convergence of first-order algorithms, without requiring full monotonicity. Yet, despite this recurring role, a systematic study of the class itself has been missing from the literature. This paper fills that gap with the first comprehensive treatment of star monotone operators, a class that strictly encompasses monotone and pseudomonotone operators with nonempty zero sets, together with operators that are strongly quasimonotone along rays and satisfy a radial nondegeneracy condition. We develop basic calculus rules, existence and uniqueness results for zeros, global metric subregularity, and precise structural relationships with classical monotonicity notions. We further demonstrate the versatility of star monotonicity through a Clarke subdifferential characterization of nonsmooth star quasiconvexity, applications to Minty and Stampacchia variational inequalities, linear convergence guarantees for subgradient-type methods, and separable operators related to the Debreu--Koopmans problem.

items.title: Subgradient and Stochastic Finite-Difference Methods for Constrained Strongly Quasiconvex Optimization
items.summary: We propose a projected subgradient method for solving quasiconvex minimization problems. By employing the Clarke subdifferential, we prove that the sequence generated by the proposed algorithm converges to a solution of the minimization problem when the objective function is locally Lipschitz continuous and strongly quasiconvex in the sense of Polyak, under the same assumptions required for convex functions with the convex subdifferential. Moreover, we derive explicit convergence rate estimates for both the iterates and objective function values. In particular, compared with the corresponding results for nonsmooth, locally Lipschitz, strongly convex optimization, our analysis replaces strong convexity with strong quasiconvexity while preserving the order of the convergence rate, thereby extending the guarantees to a class of possibly nonconvex objective functions. In addition, we investigate a stochastic finite-difference scheme for minimizing a strongly quasiconvex function subject to inequality constraints defined by strongly quasiconvex functions, and establish a convergence rate of order $O(k^{-1/4})$, consistent with known complexity bounds for stochastic zeroth-order methods.

items.title: A Monotone Meshfree-Particle Method for Mean Field Games on Scattered Point Clouds
items.summary: We develop a monotone meshfree--particle method for mean field games (MFGs). We discretize the backward Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation on a fixed scattered cloud, transport the forward Fokker--Planck law with reflected and killed particles, and close the fictitious-play loop by interpolation and mass-preserving kernel density estimation. Monotonicity is imposed row by row on two-dimensional clouds. Each row combines a positive generalized finite difference Laplacian with a nonnegative decomposition of the drift along rays to surrounding visible neighbors, with mirror images at reflecting walls, and every fixed-policy matrix is an M-matrix for arbitrary cell-Péclet number. We prove a discrete comparison principle and, on polygons with re-entrant corners included, that one HJB solve at a prescribed density converges to the viscosity solution off the boundary vertices, for convex Hamiltonians of at most quadratic growth under a structure condition. On a two-room floor plan with re-entrant door jambs, the computed HJB solutions converge to exact ones. A source-free exact MFG tests the fully coupled computation. At matched degrees of freedom on a grid domain, the meshfree HJB solve has a larger $L^2$ error and a smaller $L^\infty$ error than a five-point finite-difference solve, and is about twice as expensive including the stencil construction. On a non-convex evacuation game, the interior nodes of nine clouds receive monotone rows, apart from a few next to the boundary vertices that copy a neighbor.

items.title: Speedup-Aware Rounding for Scheduling Malleable Tasks with Precedence Constraints
items.summary: We study the scheduling of malleable tasks with precedence constraints on $m$ identical processors to minimize the makespan, assuming that the processing time of a task does not increase and its work does not decrease with the number of processors, and that the work is a convex function of the processing time. The standard two-phase method solves a linear program, rounds the fractional processing times to allotments, caps the allotments at a threshold $μ$, and runs list scheduling. We propose \emph{speedup-aware rounding}, which rounds a task to its slower allotment exactly when this allotment is at most a factor $a$ slower than the fractional processing time. We determine the worst-case increase of the work under this rule exactly and show that no per-task rounding rule with time factor $a$ does better. With $μ=\lceilβ(a)m\rceil$ the algorithm achieves the approximation ratio $13(30+\sqrt{493})/225\approx3.0162$ for every $m$, which improves the previous bound $2+\sqrt2\approx3.4142$; a single task with linear speedup shows that its ratio is at least $\approx2.9558$. For concave speedup functions, which include the roofline, communication, Amdahl and power-law models, the ratio becomes $\approx2.9739$, which improves the ratio $\approx3.2919$ of Jansen and Zhang. We also revisit the strictly decreasing case of our earlier work (Chen and Chu, 2013): the reported ratio $2.9549$ relies on an elimination step that is not valid. In this case the algorithm coincides with that of Jansen and Zhang up to its parameters, and with parameters chosen by the corrected analysis it guarantees their ratio $\approx3.2919$. Finally, without convexity no per-task rounding improves the known time--work trade-off, and the analysis cannot go below $(3+\sqrt5)/2$.

items.title: Exact Output Steering with Vanishing Controls in Weighted Shift Dynamics
items.summary: Exploiting the rich dynamics of wrapped weighted shifts and their residualizations, we characterize exact projected steering with vanishing initial controls. For wrapped shifts, steering is characterized by an expansive cycle multiplier and a residue separating the source and control channels. For residual shifts, a distinct spectral--toral mechanism emerges: steering through selected conjugate planes is equivalent to radial expansion and an arithmetic parity condition on phase resonances, yielding bounded-gap steering times and quantitative control estimates. For structured machine-learning representations built from orbit dictionaries, we derive a two-scale gain condition for steering coefficients while preserving decoded outputs.

items.title: Relative-energy stabilization of an irreversible port-Hamiltonian tubular reactor
items.summary: This paper develops a relative-energy control approach for a boundary-controlled irreversible port-Hamiltonian model of a non-isothermal tubular reactor around a spatially nonuniform stationary profile. The starting point is a thermodynamic duality between the entropy-based availability used in earlier reactor control and the relative Hamiltonian induced by the irreversible port-Hamiltonian representation. Under physically interpretable stability conditions---positive heat capacity, positive compressibility and positive compositional susceptibility---the Hamiltonian density is shown to be strictly convex, while the corresponding entropy representation is strictly concave. The resulting relative Hamiltonian decomposes into kinetic, compressive, thermal and mixing contributions and yields an exact relative-energy balance in which irreversible dissipation is separated from profile-dependent terms. This structure leads to a bounded monotone distributed jacket feedback that injects thermal damping without cancelling the nonlinear PDE dynamics. A continuous coercivity condition gives a local a-priori decay estimate for sufficiently regular nonlinear solutions, while a composite energy functional provides an exponential estimate for the linearized closed-loop initial-boundary value problem. Structure-preserving PFEM simulations are used to verify the predicted dissipation mechanisms and constrained profile regulation.

items.title: Parallel Spanning Forest and Biconnectivity for Well-Connected Graph in Sub-Logarithmic Time
items.summary: We give a randomized ARBITRARY CRCW PRAM algorithm for computing a spanning forest of an \(n\)-vertex, \(m\)-edge graph. Let \(d\) be the maximum component diameter. With good probability, the algorithm runs in \(O(\log d+\log\log n)\) time using \(O(m+n)\) processors and outputs a rooted spanning forest of original edges with maximum depth \(2^{O(\log d+\log\log n)}\). For finding bridges, our algorithm identifies every bridge edge in \(O(\log d+\log\log n)\) time. For biconnectivity, it outputs all blocks in \(O(\log d+\log d'+\log\log n)\) time, where \(d'\) is the bi-diameter. All these problems are fundamental in graph algorithms with numerous applications. Our results improve the best previous time bounds parameterized by the number of vertices and diameter. Finally, we prove deterministic \(Ω(\log n/\log\log n)\) lower bounds for outputting a DFS Sequence, a weighted spanning forest, and an ear decomposition.

items.title: Tokenization: Hardness and Bicriteria Approximation Algorithms
items.summary: We study Binary Tokenization: given a corpus of binary strings over $\{0,1\}$ and a vocabulary budget $K$, select at most $K$ substrings (called vocabulary) to minimize the total number of tokens needed to represent the corpus. The primitive symbols $0$ and $1$ are always available, and each document must be segmented separately. Letting $n$ denote the total corpus length and $M$ for the maximum document length, we prove that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, Binary Tokenization problem does not have polynomial-time $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation algorithms unless $\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{NP}$. To complement the hardness result, we give a polynomial-time $(γ,γ)$-bicriteria algorithm, with $γ= \sqrt{M}\log n$: The algorithm outputs a vocabulary of size at most $γK$ with number of tokens at most $γ{\rm OPT}_K$, where ${\rm OPT}_K$ is the optimal number of tokens under the original budget $K$. We also study a storage-budget variant, in which the sum of the selected substrings' lengths is bounded by $B$. For $2\le B<n$, we obtain an $(O(\log n\log B),O(\log n\log B))$-bicriteria approximation algorithm.

items.title: Frank-Wolfe Theorems for Mixed Integer Quadratic Optimization
items.summary: The Frank-Wolfe theorem states that a quadratic function bounded from below on a polyhedron attains its infimum. We study when this remains true in the presence of integer variables, for sets defined by quadratic inequalities. Our main result is a complete classification for sets defined by convex quadratic inequalities with rational coefficients and a rational affine hull, a condition that holds for all full- dimensional sets. One integer variable never destroys attainment: if every rational quadratic objective that is bounded from below attains its infimum over the set, even after adding rational linear constraints, the same holds with one integer variable. In dimension at most 2, integer variables never destroy attainment. In dimension at least 3 and with two or more integer variables, attainment holds for every such objective if and only if the set has bounded curvature, that is, it is bounded except along directions in which all constraints are linear. Without convexity, these results remain valid, except that bounded curvature is no longer necessary. Moreover, integer variables can destroy attainment only if there are at least two of them and at least one continuous variable. The result for one integer variable follows from a lifting theorem, which also extends known results for cubic objectives and convex polynomial constraints. Finally, for convex constraints and rational data, attainment holds when the objective is bounded from above, convex, or quasi-convex over a full-dimensional convex set containing the feasible region.

items.title: Reduced-Complexity WMMSE Approach for Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems With Finite-Capacity Fronthaul Links
items.summary: We propose a reduced-complexity weighted minimum mean squared error (R-WMMSE) framework for cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) systems with finite-capacity fronthaul links. To maximize the system capacity, we need to jointly design beamforming vectors at distributed access points (APs) and fronthaul quantization noise covariances. Such a task would be addressed using conventional WMMSE algorithms and their variants. However, existing WMMSE-based methods either assume ideal infinite-capacity fronthaul links or incur high computational complexity when jointly optimizing the network-wide beamforming and fronthaul compression variables. To this end, the proposed method jointly optimizes beamforming and fronthaul compression by leveraging a sequential per-AP optimization strategy. Since each subproblem is efficiently solved via Lagrangian duality with closed-form updates, the overall computational complexity can be significantly reduced compared to the conventional WMMSE method. To further reduce hardware cost, we extend the R-WMMSE framework to hybrid analog-digital beamforming systems, tackling the joint design of digital beamforming, fronthaul compression, and analog beamforming. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme achieves performance nearly identical to that of the conventional WMMSE while reducing the runtime by over 99%.

items.title: RPX: Certifying Agent-Generated MILP Reformulations at Scale
items.summary: We present RPX, an independent certificate checker for AI-generated reformulations of mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). RPX verifies that every feasible solution of either the original or the reformulated model can be converted into a feasible solution of the other with no worse objective value. This guarantees equal optimal values and enables solution recovery in the original variables. The checker derives the required checks directly from both models and verifies the certificate using exact arithmetic and reusable reconstruction rules. RPX certifies an agent-generated reformulation for each of the 240 instances in MIPLIB 2017 Benchmark v2. The source models contain up to 27.3 million matrix nonzeros. The median time to decode and check a certificate is 0.312 s, with a 95th percentile of 10.1 s.

items.title: Multiple-relaxation-time vectorial lattice Boltzmann schemes for incompressible flow: second-order consistency and parameter selection
items.summary: We construct and analyze multiple-relaxation-time vectorial lattice Boltzmann schemes for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in two and three space dimensions. The same moment-space relaxation matrix is applied to all physical components, with independent rates for the flux, stress, and energy moments. A Maxwell expansion organized by moment parity establishes formal second-order consistency of the unforced interior schemes under diffusive scaling, assuming a smooth near-equilibrium Maxwell branch. The viscosity depends only on the flux rate; for the two-dimensional scheme, we identify the first contributions of the stress and energy rates to the second-order macroscopic truncation error. We further construct a positive definite symmetrizer for the collision Jacobian at rest and derive an exact weighted-norm identity for the nonlinear kinetic residual under local collision. At fixed viscosity, a finite Fourier search selects the free rates by combining transverse-mode accuracy with short-wavelength damping. The resulting rates are compared with those calibrated against flow errors on a coarse grid. Numerical experiments exhibit second-order convergence and illustrate how the free rates affect spectral properties and finite-time flow errors.

items.title: $k$-Product Lists for (Generalized) Feedback Vertex Sets: A Tool for Designing FPT Algorithms
items.summary: Enumerating all inclusion-minimal solutions is a powerful approach to designing fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms. However, for the \textsc{Feedback Vertex Set} problem, this approach faces a fundamental obstacle, as the number of minimal feedback vertex sets is not, in general, bounded by any function of the solution size~$k$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a data structure called a \emph{$k$-product list}, which implicitly encodes all minimal solutions while admitting non-minimal ones to maintain efficiency. We present FPT algorithms for computing such lists not only for the \textsc{Feedback Vertex Set} problem but also for its natural generalizations, the \textsc{$\ell$-Forest Deletion Set} problem and the \textsc{$r$-Pseudoforest Deletion Set} problem. Our framework yields simple FPT algorithms for a wide range of variants, providing the first such results in several cases and demonstrating the broad applicability of our approach.

items.title: Weight-Adjusted Entropy-Stable BR2 and CDG Viscous Discretizations with Wall Boundary Conditions for Compressible Flows on Curvilinear Grids
items.summary: Entropy-stable discontinuous Galerkin schemes are known for their robustness. These schemes satisfy a semi-discrete entropy inequality, mimicking the entropy inequality of the continuous governing equations. Entropy-stable viscous discretizations with entropy-stable wall boundary conditions have been used in the literature, using a scheme similar to BR1. On the other hand, viscous discretizations with compact stencil, such as BR2 and CDG schemes, are more efficient for computation and for forming the Jacobian. Moreover, it is known that the weight-adjusted formulations have better efficiency with regard to the computational and storage costs. To that end, we derive the weight-adjusted entropy-stable BR2 and CDG schemes with modifications for the numerical flux at the boundary to account for the entropy-stable boundary conditions.

items.title: The optimization landscape of robust high-dimensional mean estimation: stability, moment adaptation, and mirror descent reweighting
items.summary: We study efficient robust estimation of a high-dimensional mean under strong contamination when the clean distribution has only $p\ge2$ moments, bounded by $ν_p$. We give a unified proof of stability for every $p\ge2$ with the optimal dimension-free sub-Gaussian rate, linking the reweighting, trimming and truncation techniques of the outlier and heavy-tailed robust literatures through concentration of counting and truncation processes. Building on stability and spectral signatures, we quantify the optimization landscape over sample weights that remove at most a fraction $\varepsilon_{n,k}=k/n$ of the mass, where the trimming parameter $k$ slightly exceeds the number of outliers. An unobserved convex spectral loss has inexact quadratic growth, with curvature $\frac{1-\varepsilon_{n,k}}{\varepsilon_{n,k}}$, relative to a mean-induced Bregman divergence, and the observable spectral loss supplies a dimension-free, inexact, relatively weakly star-convex subgradient oracle for it. This yields a Lyapunov analysis of mirror descent reweighting for $\varepsilon_{n,k}<\frac13$ that covers Hedge, the projected subgradient method, a new mean-induced mirror descent, and a centered multiplicative weights update. Each method uses one top-eigenvector computation per step and attains the optimal sub-Gaussian rate without knowledge of $(p,ν_p)$. Mean-induced mirror descent further achieves faster optimization rates and last-iterate guarantees, at the cost of a more expensive projection step in higher dimensions.

items.title: Understanding the Asymptotic Transience of Q-Learning via Distributional Expansion
items.summary: Q-learning has been empirically observed to exhibit substantial transient error. This transient remains uncaptured by the leading Gaussian limit because the central-limit normalization removes the smaller-scale displacement generated by the initial nonlinear evolution. On the other hand, worst-case finite-sample guarantees, while accounting for transient effects, can obscure the mechanisms responsible for the error on a particular problem instance. We develop a finer asymptotic analysis that gives an asymptotically exact characterization of this transient for a fixed instance. Specifically, for synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes, we separate the last-iterate error into an optimal-policy temporal-difference (TD) component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization. The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the maximization transient is of order $n^{-1}$ and converges almost surely, after rescaling by $n$, to a random limit. This limit represents the propagated effect of maximization errors generated before the greedy policy stabilizes. We combine this characterization with an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component to identify the corrections to its Gaussian approximation, separating the effects of initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations, and maximization. The results reveal how transient errors arise for individual Q-learning instances and how their effects persist below the central-limit scale.

items.title: Machine Learning Moment Closure for the Boltzmann Transport Equation: Enforcing Hyperbolicity
items.summary: The Boltzmann transport equation describes particle transport across collisional regimes, but resolving its velocity dependence is expensive. Moment methods reduce this cost by evolving finitely many velocity moments, requiring a closure for unresolved higher-order moments. Data-driven closures can represent these moments accurately, yet without structural constraints they may produce complex characteristic speeds and unstable simulations. Learned Boltzmann closures with guaranteed hyperbolicity have so far been formulated in one spatial dimension; in multiple dimensions, hyperbolicity must hold in every direction simultaneously. We develop, to the best of our knowledge, the first data-driven closure for multidimensional Hermite moment systems of the linear Boltzmann equation that is hyperbolic by construction. The network learns a symmetric positive-definite symmetrizer shared by all spatial directions and restricted to a subspace that preserves the known lower-order transport equations; the unresolved rows follow from a symmetric completion. Every directional Jacobian thus has real eigenvalues and a complete set of eigenvectors for every network output and at any truncation order. The closure is trained only on spatial derivatives of unresolved moments from kinetic reference solutions, with no solver in the training loop, and evolved by a partially conservative discontinuous Galerkin method. In two-dimensional experiments in the transition and scattering-dominated regimes, a single learned third-order system with ten moments remains stable in all cases. Averaged over time, it is more accurate than the classical P7 and P15 truncations with 36 and 136 moments in every experiment, and its density error is about two orders of magnitude smaller than that of the P3 truncation with the same moments.

items.title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
items.summary: In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tildeω(1/\varepsilon)$. We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $β\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-β}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tildeω(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.

items.title: Characterizing Local Breadth in Language Generation
items.summary: Large language models sharpen the validity--breadth trade-off: a generator should avoid hallucinations without collapsing onto a narrow set of valid outputs. We study generation from positive examples of an unknown target in the Kleinberg--Mullainathan model, with arbitrary, possibly adversarial order and no distributional or computational assumptions. Breadth is measured by lower Banach density, which rules out arbitrarily large sparse holes, unlike prefix-based lower asymptotic density. 1. Exact optima in one dimension: For each target $K$ in a countable family, we characterize its optimal lower Banach density $b(K)$ via equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations. One eventually valid generator attains all $b(K)$ simultaneously. Every $α\in[0,1/2]$ occurs as $b(K)$ in some countable family; finite Cantor--Bendixson point rank guarantees $b(K)=1/2$, even without a uniform rank bound. 2. Unavoidable trade-offs in higher dimensions: For $d\ge2$, there need not be a single best generator: optimizing density for one target may worsen the guarantee for another. An explicit family quantifies this intrinsically multi-objective trade-off. 3. Complete characterization of density profiles: We characterize the full region of simultaneously achievable guarantees, with equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations, after excluding geometrically degenerate rectangles. Every prescribed product $\prod_i[0,α_i]$, $α_i\in[0,1/2]$ can occur as an exact achievable region for some language collection. 4. Near-half guarantees and the sharp endpoint: Under a near-logarithmic nondegeneracy condition, one generator achieves filtered density at least $1/2-\varepsilon$ at all finite-point-rank targets, for every $\varepsilon>0$, improving the previous polylogarithmic threshold. The exact $1/2$ endpoint can fail even for a rank-zero singleton family.

items.title: An Inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method for Semidefinite Complementarity Optimization
items.summary: Semidefinite complementarity constraints arise in applications such as inverse semidefinite programming and rank-constrained matrix optimization. We develop a structure-preserving augmented Lagrangian method (SPALM) for mathematical programs with these constraints. The method augments the smooth constraints and retains matrix complementarity in its subproblems. We handle these subproblems by an inexact proximal alternating framework with verifiable descent and stationarity conditions. With vanishing absolute subproblem errors, feasible accumulation points of infinite outer sequences are asymptotically M-stationary. Under AM-regularity, these points are M-stationary. We prove that active-set SDCMPCC-LICQ is sufficient for this regularity. For each AL subproblem, the full stationarity residual converges to zero along infinite accepted inner sequences if the initial sublevel set is bounded, the proximal parameters are bounded above and away from zero, and the block errors vanish. If the block errors are also square-summable, an $O(T^{-1/2})$ best-residual bound holds over $T$ accepted iterations. Huber-Stiefel and fixed-basis procedures generate feasible matrix candidates, whose acceptance is verified by descent tests and computable limiting-normal certificates. For rank-constrained correlation matrix approximation, we construct a lifting that preserves the projected feasible set and global optimal value and satisfies active-set SDCMPCC-LICQ at every feasible point. The stationarity guarantees apply to this lifted model. Finite-budget experiments on this lifting and a single-equality observation-fitting inverse SDP meet the prescribed numerical feasibility and stationarity tests in all 120 runs.

items.title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
items.summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

items.title: A Novel Iterative Algorithm Incorporating Machine Learning for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck Equations in Three-Dimensional Ion Channel Simulation
items.summary: The Poisson Nernst Planck (PNP) equation is widely used to simulate ion channel transport, but its strong nonlinearity and coupling characteristics make numerical solutions extremely challenging, and decoupling methods are usually required. The Gummel iteration method is widely adopted as a common decoupling algorithm owing to its simplicity, ease of implementation, and applicability even under complex conditions. But its convergence efficiency highly depends on the selection of the relaxation parameter, unsuitable parameters will lead to slow convergence or even divergence. At present, parameter selection relies heavily on manual experience, which is inefficient and unstable, significantly hindering the solving efficiency for practical problems such as ion channel simulations. To address this, we propose a machine learning-based parameter selection method, which can select near-optimal relaxation parameters for the Gummel iteration of PNP equations for ion channels. Based on the machine learning-based parameter selection algorithm, we develop a coupled finite element and Gummel iteration solver, and more stable convergence and higher computational efficiency have been achieved in ion channel simulations. To validate the method, we conduct tests on two real channels with complex geometries that differ significantly from the training samples. Numerical results demonstrate that this method has a significant effect on improving the convergence efficiency and stability of Gummel iteration, confirming its applicability in practical ion channel simulations.

items.title: Splitting and Alternating Minimization Methods for Training Orthogonal Deep Feedforward Networks
items.summary: Training deep feedforward networks with weight matrices constrained to layer-wise Stiefel manifolds serves as an effective regularization technique to improve generalization. However, the simultaneous presence of orthogonality constraints and nonsmooth activation functions poses severe theoretical and computational challenges for standard stochastic gradient and Riemannian optimization methods. In this paper, we propose two splitting and alternating-based algorithms to train orthogonal deep feedforward networks (OrthDFNs). By introducing auxiliary variables, we decouple the nested nonsmooth compositions and manifold constraints into a structured equality-constrained optimization problem. To solve this model, we develop OrthALM, an inexact augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) that employs a proximal alternating minimization scheme to solve its subproblems. Crucially, every block coordinate subproblem admits an exact, closed-form solution. We establish a rigorous convergence theory for OrthALM, proving that every accumulation point of the generated sequence is a Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) point of the regularized, reformulated problem.
