The multiscale basis functions are the harmonic extensions of a fixed set of boundary traces, each a Galerkin solve in that space. Shared interface traces enforce continuity, larger blocks are assembled by recursive static condensation without any parent-scale network, and a localized Céa bound attributes the error of the learned spaces primitive by primitive. The training labels are harmonic responses of single patches, so no global solve enters the training. Against MsFEM, GMsFEM, the neural-operator element method and an end-to-end Fourier neural operator, Ms-LegONet is the most accurate at equal unknowns: its $L^2$ error is $4$ to $150$ times below the baselines on two-dimensional mosaics of $256$ high-contrast primitives, and its median error stays within $0.1$ percentage points of that of exact local spaces in three-dimensional layered media. For each new coefficient it is $1.6$ to $2.3$ times faster than a fine-grid direct solve in two dimensions. In three dimensions it computes the many-query port response of a chain $30$ to $900$ times faster than finite element solves on the same or a finer mesh, at a relative error of $10^{-4}$ against their $6\%$ and $1.6\%$.

items.title: Impact of Reduced-Order Modelling on Sum-of-Squares Region-of-Attraction Certification for Grid-Forming and Grid-Following Converters
items.summary: With the increasing penetration of power-electronic equipment, the transient stability of grid-forming (GFM) and grid-following (GFL) converters is increasingly characterized through the region of attraction (ROA) of the post-fault equilibrium. Sum-of-squares (SOS) programming yields certified inner approximations of the ROA, yet its computational cost grows rapidly with system order. Reduced-order models are therefore widely used to reduce computational cost and, more importantly, to enable analytical investigation. However, ROA analyses based on these models often assume that reproducing the converter's transient response, or retaining more dynamics in the correct time-frame, is sufficient to preserve the ROA of the full-order system. Using time-domain ODE simulations as a reference, the SOS-based ROA of each reduced-order GFM and GFL model is assessed against both its own simulated ROA and that of the corresponding full-order model, thereby separating SOS-induced conservativeness from model-order-induced ROA distortion. The results indicate that increasing reduced-order model complexity does not necessarily improve SOS-based ROA fidelity. In the cases examined, more complex reduced-order models yield lower SOS coverage of the full-order reference ROA, despite closer ODE-boundary agreement in some regions. Model selection should therefore consider both full-order ROA fidelity and certified coverage of the practical operating range, rather than model complexity alone.

items.title: Pseudo-marginal Sampling for Selective Inference
items.summary: Inference after adaptive selection must account for selection bias. One approach is to condition on the selected event, but for complex selection procedures, the resulting conditional distribution can be analytically intractable and require sampling-based methods. Rejection sampling provides a natural baseline: it repeatedly draws from a proposal and retains only samples that reproduce the observed selection. This can be prohibitively expensive when the selection event is rare. We address this computational bottleneck with a pseudo-marginal Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that samples from the selective distribution. Using a weak Poincaré inequality, we analyze its computational efficiency relative to rejection sampling and identify when it can offer substantial gains. In the classical file-drawer problem, we derive precise computational costs for both methods, illustrating exponential improvement as the selection event becomes increasingly rare. In numerical experiments involving complex selection procedures without tractable conditional distributions, the pseudo-marginal sampler is often hundreds of times more efficient than rejection sampling, while the resulting tests achieve nominal selective Type I error.

items.title: Euclidean Hulls of Double Cyclic Codes of Arbitrary Block Lengths
items.summary: Gao et al. \cite{GWF23} recently explored the Euclidean hulls of double cyclic codes over $\mathbb{Z}_2$. While they found answers for non-separable codes with coprime lengths ($\gcd(r, s) = 1$), the non-coprime case ($\gcd(r, s) > 1$) remained an open question. This paper completely solves that problem for all possible block lengths. We calculate the exact generator polynomials for the hull and show the precise conditions needed for a non-separable code to turn into a separable one. Using this, we show how to construct non-separable LCD codes. We also include several numerical examples to confirm our findings.

items.title: Fragment-Free Constraint Programming for the Preemptive Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem
items.summary: This article addresses the preemptive flexible job shop scheduling problem with makespan minimization (FJm | pmtn | C_max). We propose an exact constraint programming approach that completely avoids representing the processing fragments of an operation. Operations are placed in flexible time windows, where Horn's workload condition guarantees feasible preemptive scheduling, and Jackson's preemptive earliest-deadline-first rule reconstructs exact processing segments post-optimization in O(n log n) time per machine. To manage undecided machine assignments, we extend the PreemptiveNoOverlap global constraint to optional intervals within IBM ILOG CP Optimizer, performing overload checking and preemptive edge-finding in O(n log n) time while eliminating infeasible machine alternatives. The CP model is warm-started using a multi-round MILP assignment relaxation with Carlier's head-tail bounds and a window-based greedy heuristic. Extensive computational experiments on 276 pFJSSP benchmark instances and 78 pJSSP instances demonstrate that the proposed method significantly advances the state of the art. Within a 600~s time limit, it improves the upper bounds of the previously published logic-based Benders decomposition by 3.6% on average, increases the number of proven optimal pFJSSP instances from 102 to 180, and closes 74 instances for the first time (including the entire Barnes family). On the pJSSP under identical hardware conditions, it proves 67 of 78 instances optimal (compared to 51 by the baseline solver Mistral) and closes 9 of the 11 long-standing open problems.

items.title: Weak convergence orders for a fully discrete approximation of semilinear stochastic PDEs driven by multiplicative Gaussian and Poisson noise
items.summary: This paper investigates the weak convergence of a fully discrete approximation for a class of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) driven by multiplicative Gaussian and Poisson noise. The scheme combines a spectral Galerkin discretization in space with an exponential Euler discretization in time. Compared with single-noise settings, the simultaneous presence of continuous and jump perturbations introduces additional challenges arising from discontinuous trajectories, nonlocal jump operators, and their interaction with state-dependent multiplicative coefficients. To overcome these difficulties, we establish the exponential integrability of the numerical solution processes and refined moment estimates in negative Sobolev norms for the associated first- and second-order variational processes. Combining these estimates with a discrete-time approximation argument and Wiener--Poisson Malliavin calculus, we derive regularity estimates for the solutions of the Kolmogorov equations associated with the spatial Galerkin approximations. Based on these estimates, we obtain the temporal and spatial weak convergence orders arbitrarily close to one with respect to discretization parameters $τ$ and $λ_N^{-1}$, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first weak convergence result for a fully discrete approximation of semilinear SPDEs with simultaneous multiplicative Gaussian and Poisson noise.

items.title: Complete Decentralization of Wave Equation Control on a Compact Domain
items.summary: A feedback control policy is completely decentralized if the actuation signal at each location in space can be computed based only on state information from that location. For systems equipped with large numbers of spatially distributed sensors and actuators, completely decentralized controllers are desirable since they can be implemented in a communication and computation efficient manner, but generally perform worse than centralized counterparts. However, through a case study of Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) design for wave dynamics on a compact spatial domain, we show that careful design of system parameters to satisfy certain conditions causes a decentralized control policy to perform as well as any centralized policy. We then propose a spatially filtered $H_2$ norm to show that satisfying these conditions does not inherently degrade achievable closed-loop system performance, enabling simultaneous realization of both desirable performance and communication/computation efficiency via system-control co-design. Additional robustness analysis characterizes a range of system parameters such that the system interconnected with a decentralized controller maintains stability and near-optimal performance. Although our framework is derived for spatially continuous dynamics, we demonstrate that this theory can be leveraged to derive results for decentralization in finite-dimensional settings through a damped mass-spring example.

items.title: Minimum Synthesis Time for Single-Deletion Correcting Codes of Prescribed Size
items.summary: DNA is a promising medium for data storage, but the high cost of DNA synthesis remains a major obstacle to its widespread deployment. In the reference-based synthesis model, synthesis time is measured by the length of the reference sequence. Previous studies have analyzed code sizes under synthesis-time constraints and constructed cost-constrained codes, including codes that correct deletions. In this paper, we study the minimum synthesis time for codes of prescribed size, considering both unrestricted codes and single-deletion correcting codes. We establish finite-length lower bounds valid for arbitrary reference sequences and upper bounds using existing $q$-ary differential VT codes. For fixed $q\geq3$, $A>0$, and $R\in(0,1)$, we determine the minimum synthesis time up to an $O(1)$ term when the code size is $M_n=\lfloor Aq^{Rn}\rfloor$. The corresponding redundancy is $(1-R)n\log_2q-\log_2A+o(1)$ bits. In particular, for these code sizes, the minimum synthesis time for single-deletion correcting codes exceeds that for unrestricted codes by a term proportional to $\ln n$, and we determine its coefficient. We also derive upper and lower bounds for code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^{s_n})\rfloor$, where $s_n\to\infty$ and $s_n=o(n)$. These sizes correspond to redundancy $\log_2 n+s_n\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. For code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^c)\rfloor$ with fixed constant $c$, the redundancy is $\log_2 n+c\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. We give conditions under which single-deletion correcting codes exist or do not exist for all sufficiently large $n$, together with bounds on the minimum synthesis time. These results show how code size and the single-deletion correcting constraint affect synthesis time and provide theoretical guidance for the construction of cost-constrained codes.

items.title: Boundary-controlled irreversible port--Hamiltonian modeling and structure-preserving discretization of tubular reactors
items.summary: This paper presents a boundary-controlled irreversible port-Hamiltonian model and a structure-preserving spatial discretization for a non-isothermal tubular reactor with axial convection, variable-density momentum dynamics, chemical reaction, mass diffusion, heat conduction, and jacket heat transfer. Reaction, diffusion, and heat conduction are described by irreversible port-Hamiltonian channels, whereas convection and momentum are represented by a weighted Eulerian interconnection. The boundary ports recover the axial energy flux and the corresponding entropy flux. A partitioned finite-element method is then formulated in conservative coordinates using a power-preserving change of variables. The semi-discrete model satisfies the Hamiltonian balance and a discrete entropy balance with non-negative entropy production due to reaction, diffusion, heat conduction, and jacket heat transfer. Numerical results for an open tubular reactor are validated against independently computed continuous steady boundary-value solutions and show the transient temperature, composition, and velocity profiles in the very-low-Mach regime. The same discretization is also tested with reciprocal Soret--Dufour coupling, for which the discrete entropy production remains non-negative.

items.title: Neumann Series of Bessel Functions for a Quadratic Sturm--Liouville Pencil
items.summary: We construct Neumann series of Bessel functions representations for solutions and their first derivatives of the equation $-y^{\prime\prime}(x)+(q(x)+2ρp(x))y(x)=ρ^2y(x)$. The series arise from Legendre expansions of two transmutation operator kernels. The obtained series converge uniformly on horizontal strips in the complex plane of the parameter $ρ$. We develop a recursive integration procedure for computing the coefficients of these representations. The knowledge of the first coefficients allows one to recover the potentials $p$ and $q$ which is useful for solving inverse problems. For separated boundary conditions, we estimate the characteristic functions whose zeros determine the eigenvalues. Two numerical examples illustrate the practical applicability of the obtained series representations to the solution of spectral problems.

items.title: Minimum Membership Dominating Set and Its Generalization: Leafage vs. Asteroidal Number
items.summary: The Dominating Set problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by leafage, a structural graph parameter defined on chordal graphs. We investigate whether this tractability extends to its variants with natural constraints. Specifically, we study the Minimum Membership Dominating Set problem and its generalization, the Min. $(σ, ρ)$-Dominating Set problem. Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $\ell$, Minimum Membership Dominating Set asks whether there is a dominating set $D$ such that every vertex in $G$ is dominated by at most $\ell$ vertices in $D$. We first show a negative result: Minimum Membership Dominating Set parameterized by leafage plus $\ell$ is W[1]-hard, demonstrating that even this natural constraint serves as a severe barrier to designing FPT algorithms. To complement this, we present an XP algorithm for the Min. $(σ, ρ)$-Dominating Set problem parameterized by asteroidal number plus $μ$, where $σ$ and $ρ$ are finite sets of non-negative integers and $μ$ is the maximum value in $σ\cup ρ$. Note that asteroidal number generalizes leafage to arbitrary graphs. Combining this algorithm with our structural bound that every graph $G$ admits a dominating set such that no vertex is dominated by more than $7\mathsf{an}(G)-6$ vertices, where $\mathsf{an}(G)$ denotes the asteroidal number of $G$, we show that Minimum Membership Dominating Set admits an XP algorithm parameterized solely by asteroidal number.

items.title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
items.summary: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

items.title: Uniform symmetric spectral finiteness of semialgebraic cones
items.summary: Cone-constrained eigenvalues of a matrix are defined through a complementarity problem constrained by a closed convex cone. We show that every closed semialgebraic convex cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite; that is, the cone spectra, the sets of the cone-constrained eigenvalues, of symmetric matrices relative to the cone are uniformly finite with respect to the matrices. The uniform bound is explicit, and as an application, we derive a uniform bound for the cardinality of spectra of symmetric matrices relative to Löwner cones. In addition, using the uniform finiteness of cone spectra, we also show the uniform finiteness of the number of singular values relative to two closed semialgebraic convex cones. For non-semialgebraic cones, we observe two contrasting phenomena. On the one hand, we show that the exponential cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite. On the other hand, we provide a closed non-semialgebraic convex cone such that the associated cone spectra of symmetric matrices are finite but are not uniformly finite.

items.title: Closed-Form Gaussian Information Projection for Embedded Simplices and Simplicial Mixtures
items.summary: We study Gaussian approximation of Dirichlet--Gaussian probability density functions on embedded simplices. We derive the unique information projection onto the family of nondegenerate ambient Gaussian probability density functions, obtaining closed-form expressions for the optimal Gaussian and the minimum divergence for arbitrary positive Dirichlet parameters. The minimum divergence depends only on the intrinsic simplex dimension and Dirichlet parameters, is invariant up to an affine isomorphism, independent of the ambient dimension, and independent of the normal covariance. Furthermore, by joint convexity of Kullback--Leibler divergence, we establish explicit intrinsic dimension-dependent sharp upper bounds for finite Gaussian Mixture with shared component weights. For uniform probability density functions, these bounds reduce to dimension-dependent constants. The results provide closed-form Gaussian Mixture constructions and rigorous approximation guarantees for probability density functions associated with embedded simplicial complexes. A numerical example on a circular curve illustrates the theoretical results and their connections to geometric Gaussian Mixture representations.

items.title: Branching Pattern Modeling: A Geometric Measure Theory Approach
items.summary: This article is based on a lecture given at Westlake University. It aims to introduce students to an application of geometric measure theory in modeling branched patterns found in both living and nonliving systems. We begin with the Eulerian framework of ramified optimal transportation, including discrete transport paths, their basic properties, numerical approximation, and the passage to general transport paths represented by rectifiable currents. We then describe an application to the dynamic formation of a plant leaf, where branching venation patterns arise from a balance between metabolic benefit and transportation cost. Finally, we review landscape functions associated with transport paths and explain how two existing approaches can be unified within a broader family of rectifiable $1$-currents. We conclude by indicating several open directions related to Gilbert-type network problems, biological modeling, and numerical approximation.

items.title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
items.summary: A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most HPC workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates some of those claims and explores the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads, across a variety of common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy requirements of these workloads. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations of these approaches. These results indicate that Ozaki emulation should not be evaluated as a general replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-shaped. Our analysis indicates this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Furthermore, even in this favorable regime, standalone GEMM speedup is not enough to accelerate (or avoid performance regression) for the application: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale. This paper characterizes those boundaries empirically. Furthermore, we show that dense GEMM accounts for only a small fraction of FP64 computation across HPC workloads, leaving most application-level FP64 work beyond the reach of GEMM-based emulation.

items.title: A Second-Order Parallel Neumann-Robin Splitting for the Stokes-Biot System with a Linear Time-Step Restriction
items.summary: In this paper we develop a second-order, fully decoupled, non-iterative partitioned method for the time-dependent Stokes--Biot problem on fixed domains. In previous work \cite{WangLeeCanic2026SecondOrder}, a Robin--Robin scheme with these features was introduced, and its stability and error estimates were established under the sufficient parabolic CFL-type condition $Δt\lesssim C_*h^2$. The main improvement of the new scheme is weakening the CFL-type condition to a linear CFL-type condition $Δt \lesssim C_*h$. This can be achieved with a new splitting approach by replacing the poroelastic mechanical normal Robin condition by its physical Neumann-type traction condition, which results in a Neumann--Robin splitting. For fixed coefficients satisfying the stated assumptions, we prove a fully discrete energy bound under a restriction of $Δt\lesssim C_*h$. The improvement over the parabolic restriction in the earlier Robin--Robin analysis follows from eliminating the interface residual that requires two inverse-trace estimates. We also establish an energy-norm error bound of order $h^k+Δt^2$ under explicit regularity, finite element approximation, and initialization assumptions. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions examine spatial and temporal accuracy and compare the Neumann--Robin and Robin--Robin schemes. A 3D cylindrical pressure-pulse benchmark further investigates their numerical stability behavior. The results distinguish the less restrictive sufficient stability condition established analytically from the observed stability thresholds of the two schemes.

items.title: Function Inversion Reporting
items.summary: In the Function Inversion problem, the goal is to invert a function $f:[N] \to [N]$ in two phases. In the preprocessing phase, the offline algorithm computes an advice string of length $S$ bits. In the online phase, the online algorithm receives the advice and a challenge $y \in [N]$, and the goal is to find a preimage $x \in [N]$ such that $f(x) = y$ in time $T$. The problem was initially studied in cryptography, but in recent years it has found various applications to data structure problems. Yet, several of the applications require a variant of Function Inversion, known as Function Inversion Reporting, where the goal is to output all preimages of the challenge $y$. In this paper, we study the Function Inversion Reporting problem in a systematic way by unifying and improving existing algorithms. As a result, we obtain improved data structures for several problems including 3SUM-Indexing Reporting, Range Reporting, Approximate Nearest Neighbor, Jumbled Indexing Reporting, and Gapped String Indexing Reporting.

items.title: Implicit DeepReach Without Implicit Differentiation
items.summary: We consider the problem of approximating backward reachable and reach-avoid tubes for high-dimensional nonlinear systems whose Hamiltonians require numerical optimization over constrained controls and disturbances. Existing neural Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability methods alleviate the dimensionality bottleneck of grid-based solvers, but evaluating Hamiltonians without closed-form expressions introduces an additional computational challenge. We show that, under suitable assumptions, the gradients required for value-function training can be computed without differentiating through the inner optimization problem. Specifically, we establish an envelope-type gradient identity for the saddle point Hamiltonian, under which the optimal control and disturbance enter backpropagation as constants without gradient tracking. This enables end-to-end neural HJ reachability with numerically evaluated Hamiltonians while avoiding both solver unrolling and implicit differentiation. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed approach on nonlinear reachability and reach-avoid problems of different scales.

items.title: An Accelerated Power Method
items.summary: An Accelerated Power Method (APM) for locating the dominant eigen-pair of a real, symmetric matrix is presented. The algorithm is motivated by Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Method (AGM) and a connection between the APM and the AGM holds, that is analogous to the relationship between the Conjugate Gradient and Lanczos methods. Theoretical convergence analysis shows that the APM is guaranteed to recover the dominant eigen-pair of a normalized semi-definite matrix at a rate no worse than the Power Method. For normalized indefinite matrices, the APM will recover an extremal eigen-pair, but not necessarily the dominant one, and the rate can be worse than the vanilla PM, depending upon the choice of acceleration parameter. Computational practicalities are discussed, including parameter tuning, and numerical experiments are also presented.

items.title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
items.summary: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.

items.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
items.summary: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

items.title: Optimality Guarantees for Minimum Variance Subset Selection via Semidefinite Programming
items.summary: Given a set of data points in Euclidean space and a prescribed cardinality $k$, the minimum variance $k$-subset problem asks for $k$ points minimizing their average squared distance from their centroid. We develop a semidefinite programming (SDP) framework for exact recovery and global optimization. First, we show that the natural SDP relaxation fails Slater's condition. Identifying the proper face containing its feasible region yields an equivalent, lower-dimensional, strictly feasible formulation that enjoys strong duality. A primal--dual characterization of optimality then gives geometric necessary and sufficient conditions under which the SDP relaxation is guaranteed to be tight. These conditions reveal how tightness depends on the internal geometry of the selected subset and on its separation from the remaining points. Second, we embed the SDP relaxation in a branch-and-cut algorithm combining first-order optimization, valid inequalities and dimension-reducing branching. Extensive experiments on public data sets, with up to 1,500 points and different values of $k$, show that the method strongly outperforms general-purpose exact solvers as the number of points and cardinality increase.

items.title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
items.summary: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

items.title: Patch LegONet: Resolving Localized High-Frequency PDE Dynamics with Low-Frequency Operator Blocks
items.summary: Localized interfaces, layers, and shocks can require high spatial resolution even when most of a partial differential equation (PDE) solution remains smooth. In global spectral methods, resolving these features requires increasing the approximation order across the entire domain. LegONet builds PDE solvers from reusable mechanism blocks, but its global coefficient representation faces the same limitation. We introduce Patch LegONet, which reuses pretrained mechanism blocks on smaller physical patches to resolve localized fine scales. The solution consists of a global background and local corrections. Mapping a fixed reference representation onto smaller patches increases local resolution without enlarging the blocks. The corrections join smoothly to the global background at patch boundaries. Differential operators are rescaled analytically to account for each patch's physical size. Nonlinear mechanisms are evaluated on the combined solution to include interactions between the background and local corrections. Patches can move, merge, or be removed during rollout while the pretrained patch blocks remain frozen. Six experiments on Allen-Cahn and viscous Burgers equations assess static, multiple, and moving patches in one to three dimensions. At comparable numbers of degrees of freedom, Patch LegONet consistently lowers the final relative solution error compared with global refinement. The reduction is approximately one order of magnitude in most tests. These results extend mechanism reuse across spatial scales and provide a practical route to local refinement in learned PDE solvers.

items.title: RALES: A Risk-Averse Augmented Lagrangian Equality-Constrained SQP Method
items.summary: This paper develops RALES, an augmented Lagrangian method for risk-averse optimization in function spaces with nonsmooth risk measures, nonlinear equality constraints, and convex geometric constraints. The method combines safeguarded risk and constraint multiplier updates with efficient sequential quadratic programming based on inexact subproblem solves. The analysis establishes asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems and gives conditions for feasibility of weak primal accumulation points. Under additional assumptions on subproblem accuracy, duality, and boundedness, it provides global primal optimality guarantees and weak convergence of the full stored and candidate multiplier sequences to a common dual maximizer. Dual convergence is strong when all penalty parameters remain bounded. Numerical experiments for a finitely sampled semilinear PDE control problem, with the Conditional Value-at-Risk and the Mean-Plus-Semideviation risk measures, illustrate the method's performance as the spatial mesh is refined and as the number of samples increases.

items.title: Convergence of an adaptive multilevel stochastic Galerkin FEM driven by a residual-based error estimator
items.summary: In this paper we analyze a residual-based a posteriori error estimation strategy and adaptive multilevel algorithms for a class of parametric elliptic PDEs, where the diffusion coefficient depends on countably many uncertainty parameters. Under a saturation assumption on the parametric approximation space, we propose a computable residual-based error estimator. We also introduce the notion of K-compatibility of finite element meshes, which ensures that only the triangulations with comparable mesh sizes are used, and incorporate this concept into the adaptive algorithm. We prove that the estimator is reliable and satisfies K-dependent stability and reduction properties. These results underpin our convergence analysis of the adaptive multilevel algorithm: we show that the algorithm drives both the a posteriori error estimator and the true approximation error to zero. Numerical experiments illustrate and confirm the theoretical findings.

items.title: A Fast Algorithm for Subspace Convolution
items.summary: A cornerstone result in Boolean lattice theory is the subset-zeta transform, which computes the $f$-weighted subset summation problem $(Z f)(B)=\sum_{A\subseteq B}f(A)$ for all $ B\subseteq[n]$ in $O(N \log N)$ additions instead of the naïve $O(3^n) = O(N^{\log_2 3})$, where $N=2^n$. This paper studies the algebraic analogue of this problem--the subspace summation problem--where subsets are replaced by linear subspaces in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Surprisingly, we show that this problem admits a similar $Θ_q(N_q \log N_q)$-time algorithm, where $N_q$ is the number of subspaces. This improves substantially (in both theory and practice) over lattice-based algorithms ([BHK+16, KKW16]), which are known to be optimal for addition-only algorithms over $\mathbb R$. We prove similar runtimes for inversion, rank-constrained sums and span convolution. We describe two main applications: Fast linear algebra on Grassmann graphs: Matrix--vector multiplication for arbitrary distance-invariant kernels on $N$-vertex Grassmann graphs in $O_q(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations, together with fast spectral projections and exact solutions of the corresponding linear systems. Graph coloring of low binary cut-rank graphs: An $n^{2^{r^2/4+O(1)}}$-time algorithm for computing the chromatic number and chromatic polynomial of an $n$-vertex graph, given a rank-decomposition of width $r$. We also give quantitative reductions from satisfiability and monotone constraint problems. Experiments show speedups in measured running time of up to $18$ over the covering-pair algorithm for the zeta transform, $190$ over Poisson summation for rank-constrained sums, and $22$ over the distance-matrix recurrence for Grassmann kernel multiplication. Lean 4 formalizations of the transform identities, arithmetic operation bounds, and graph-coloring constructions accompany the paper [PW26].

items.title: Combinatorial optimization with bounded subdeterminants
items.summary: We take a first step toward a broader study of classical combinatorial optimization problems through the maximum subdeterminants of their standard integer programming formulations, yielding new positive results for several famous (NP-hard) problems. An integer matrix is totally $Δ$-modular if every square submatrix has determinant of absolute value at most $Δ$. For every fixed $Δ$, it has been known that maximum clique, maximum stable set, and minimum vertex cover can be solved in polynomial time on instances for which the coefficient matrix of the natural formulation is totally $Δ$-modular. We extend this list by showing that the same holds for many other problems, including the weighted versions of maximum cut, the traveling salesman problem, feedback vertex set, odd cycle transversal, dominating set, max 2-sat, induced matching, and cluster vertex deletion, as well as for $k$-colorability and graph isomorphism. Our proofs reveal several new ways in which bounded subdeterminants impose combinatorial structure: they bound the size or maximum degree of the input graph, bound packings of cycles and other obstructions, or yield decompositions into tractable graph classes such as forests, chordal graphs, graphs of bounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded linear mim-width.

items.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
items.summary: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.

items.title: Reliable Computation of the $L_{\infty}$-Norm of Linear Time-Invariant Systems Depending on One Parameter
items.summary: The $L_{\infty}$-norm of a linear time-invariant system is a central quantity in robust control, used in robust stability tests, stability margins, and $H_{\infty}$ controller design. Physical models depend on parameters, such as masses, stiffnesses, or gains, so the $L_{\infty}$-norm becomes a function of these parameters. This computation reduces to studying the real critical points of a plane algebraic curve whose coefficients depend on the parameters. Previous approaches based on cylindrical algebraic decomposition describe the $L_{\infty}$-norm on the whole parameter space, but their cost grows very quickly with the number of parameters. In this paper, we propose instead to compute a generic parametrisation of the solutions, valid outside an explicitly characterised set of non-generic parameter values. In the case of one parameter, this parametrisation is obtained by interpolation from a certified solver for the non-parametric case. The resulting algorithm is fully certified, relying on a priori bounds and multimodular computations rather than on Gröbner bases. It is illustrated on examples from the robust control literature.

items.title: DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight
items.summary: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/

items.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
items.summary: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

items.title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
items.summary: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.

items.title: Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks
items.summary: Much of the variation in financial time series is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be predicted from an asset's own history. Per-asset self-supervised learning treats this variation as irreducible noise. Under a latent factor model, we show that conditioning prediction on the realized market factor makes the asset's market exposure necessary for optimal prediction, while reducing the noise against which the asset-specific component is learned. Building on this insight, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series. During training, we construct a leave-one-out market condition for each asset from the future target embeddings of other assets and incorporate it through factor loadings derived from the asset's own representation. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the strongest and most statistically significant gains in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the best RankIC on all liquidity targets and on return horizons from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines, and delivers the best portfolio performance in a historical backtest. Ablations show that the return and exposure gains require the condition to be aligned with the realized market movement. After restoring the volatility scale removed by normalization, the predictor's factor loadings rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as a supervised probe, without labels. A synthetic factor-model study with known parameters shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both market exposure and the asset-specific component.

items.title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control
items.summary: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

items.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
items.summary: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

items.title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
items.summary: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.

items.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
items.summary: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

items.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
items.summary: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

items.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
items.summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

items.title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
items.summary: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

items.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output (ΔH), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.

items.title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
items.summary: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π_{0.5} and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

items.title: Longtail-SWE: High-Quality SWE Tasks for Underrepresented Languages
items.summary: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.

items.title: InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure
items.summary: While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to 2.75times and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from 17.4% to 30.0%, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.

items.title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least 1.93times as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality 1.62times sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd

items.title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
items.summary: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga

items.title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
items.summary: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

items.title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
items.summary: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

items.title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
items.summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

items.title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone
items.summary: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

items.title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
items.summary: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness

items.title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
items.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens.
