items.title: DMP-Oriented Anisotropic Mesh Adaptation for SUPG Finite Element Methods for Time-Dependent Convection-Diffusion Problems
items.summary: We study discrete bound preservation for fully discrete piecewise-linear streamline upwind Petrov--Galerkin (SUPG) finite element approximations of time-dependent convection--diffusion equations on anisotropic triangular meshes. Although the continuous homogeneous-source problem satisfies a parabolic maximum principle, SUPG approximations can exhibit nonphysical undershoots and overshoots. We derive sufficient nodal discrete maximum principle (DMP) conditions that account for the stabilized mass matrix, the combined effects of physical and streamline diffusion, time-step restrictions, and transfer between successive meshes. The analysis identifies a SUPG-effective diffusion tensor and motivates an anisotropic metric aligned with its inverse. We construct a combined metric that retains the effective-tensor geometry while introducing solution-dependent mesh density through recovered Hessian information. The resulting DMP conditions provide a theoretical basis for anisotropic mesh design. Numerical experiments for time-dependent transport problems with isotropic and moderately anisotropic diffusion demonstrate that, under mass-compatible limited SUPG stabilization, the combined metric substantially reduces measured undershoots relative to other methods at matched nominal mesh budgets, although improved bound behavior can carry an accuracy penalty. A controlled tensor--density comparison in the anisotropic transport test supports a contribution from the effective tensor beyond the prescribed mesh density.

items.title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
items.summary: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \fracπ{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.

items.title: Optimal Sampling and Transmission Policy for Information Freshness in Gossip Networks
items.summary: We study the optimal sampling and transmission policies for a transmitter communicating with n gossiping receivers with the objective of tracking a source's status over time using a semantic freshness metric: Version Age of Information (VAoI). The transmitter observes the version changes in the source, and can acquire a new information version by paying a sampling cost. The receivers gossip, allowing information exchange among each other without direct transmission. Gossiping can save on transmission cost, but it may propagate stale version information, necessitating transmitter intervention. With imperfect communication links, we formulate an infinite horizon average cost Markov Decision Process (MDP) in order to jointly optimize receivers' VAoIs, sampling and transmission costs in a time slotted fully connected (FC) gossip network. We first solve the MDP using Relative Value Iteration (RVI) algorithm. Then, we prove that the sampling decision has a threshold structure in the transmitter VAoI. Further, under reliable gossiping links, we show that transmission and idling has an VAoI-difference threshold structure with minimum VAoI activation. Numerical results obtained using RVI show that the optimal policy consistently outperforms natural baselines. These results characterize how source sampling, direct transmission, and receiver gossip should be jointly coordinated for cost-aware semantic freshness in gossip networks.

items.title: Positivity Proofs for Third-Order Holonomic Sequences via Differences Scaled by Rational Functions
items.summary: We study the positivity of sequences $f$ that satisfy a third-order holonomic recurrence $f(n+3)= P_2(n) f(n+2) + P_1(n) f(n+1) + P_0(n) f(n)$ whose coefficients $P_0$, $P_1$ and $P_2$ are rational functions in $\R(x)$. We provide a sufficient condition on $P_0$, $P_1$ and $P_2$ for the recurrence to admit a solution all but finitely many terms of which are positive, and whose positivity is robust under small perturbations of the initial values. This sufficient condition is also a necessary condition for a subclass of the recurrences. By developing the proof of this sufficient condition, for another subclass of the recurrences, we show that it is decidable whether all the terms of a given sequence are positive for any initial values outside an exceptional plane. It is common to construct a positivity certificate, which guarantees the positivity of a solution, to show this kind of decidability. In this paper, we construct a new type of positivity certificate via the $S$-scaled difference $f(n+1) - S(n) f(n)$ for a suitable $S \in \R(x)$. This result partially improves the work by Ibrahim and Salvy.

items.title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
items.summary: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.

items.title: Hypervolume-based column-and-constraint generation for bi-objective two-stage robust mixed-integer programs
items.summary: Extending column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) for two-stage robust mixed-integer programs from the single-objective to the bi-objective setting is challenging: for a fixed first-stage decision and scenario, the second stage yields an entire nondominated set rather than a single objective value. We develop a C&CG algorithm that uses the hypervolume indicator - one of the most widely studied quality indicators in multi-objective optimization - to evaluate these sets and seeks a first-stage decision maximizing the worst-case hypervolume over a finite set of scenarios. To avoid the nonlinearities of an exact hypervolume formulation, we introduce a slab decomposition of the objective space that yields a linear mixed-integer master problem with an explicit bound on the discretization error. This bound enables a computable optimality-gap certificate and supports an adaptive algorithm that alternates between adding scenarios and refining the decomposition. We prove the correctness of the algorithm and establish sufficient conditions for its finite termination. Computational experiments on two-stage robust selection and assignment problems show that only a small number of scenarios need to be included in the master problem, even when the full scenario set contains 128 scenarios. Moreover, we identify the number of initial slabs as a key factor influencing the running time and develop a simple, instance-dependent rule for choosing the initial slab width that outperforms fixed choices on average for the selection problem and remains competitive for the assignment problem.

items.title: Online Imitation Learning for Stabilizing Vlasov--Poisson Plasmas
items.summary: We study the problem of controlling instability in the Vlasov--Poisson plasma systems, a fundamental challenge for nuclear fusion control. Motivated by the partial observability of plasma states in practice, we investigate imitation learning algorithms that learn from a fully-observable expert controller, but operate under macroscopic measurements. We theoretically establish a separation between online and offline imitation learning --- even a small behavior cloning error leads to error compounding that exponentially amplifies instability over time. By way of contrast, the online imitation learning loss can polynomially control the stability of rollout trajectories. We then propose a DAgger-style algorithm that learns the stabilizing controller under partial observability. Simulation results on a 1D Vlasov--Poisson system demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively stabilize plasma instabilities over longer time horizons than behavior cloning.

items.title: Neural Operator Surrogates for Landweber Iteration in Solving Inverse Problems
items.summary: Neural operators can accurately approximate well-posed mappings, but for unbounded or discontinuous operators, common in inverse problems, we verify that their network parameters often blow up in architectures such as DeepONet and FNO. To solve inverse problems stably, we use Landweber iteration, which requires only a forward map and the adjoint of its derivative (linearisation). To reduce repeated PDE forward evaluations, we replace the forward operator and its derivative with a differentiable neural-operator surrogate. We show that encoder-network-decoder operators, including generalised DeepONets and fully coupled Fourier operators, approximate both the forward map and its derivative. A modified discrepancy principle ensures decreasing error before finite stopping. With a compact preconditioner, the iterates remain in a compact set where accurate surrogates exist, and the stopped reconstructions converge as data and surrogate errors vanish under a regularity condition. We also relate the theory to derivative-informed training along finite directions, showing that the preconditioner determines which derivative errors affect the Landweber iteration update. Experiments on identifying a reaction coefficient in an elliptic equation show that smoothing reduces late-iteration deterioration for less accurate surrogates but slows sharp-feature recovery, and that smaller derivative errors along training directions do not by themselves improve reconstruction accuracy.

items.title: Representing Tensors as Compositions for Efficient Computation on Sparse and Structured Data
items.summary: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.

items.title: Efficient SC-Flip Decoding for Polar Codes through Decision-Boundary Normalization
items.summary: Accurate first erroneous position (FEP) identification is key to improving the error-correction performance of successive cancellation flip (SCF) decoding. However, FEP identification remains challenging with a limited number of re-decoding attempts. To address this issue, we propose decision-boundary normalization (DBN) to improve FEP identification and develop a novel DBN-SCF decoding algorithm. DBN normalizes the magnitude of each decision log-likelihood ratio (LLR) by the standard deviation predicted by the Gaussian approximation (GA) for the corresponding bit-channel. This allows a single normalized threshold to be shared across bit-channels within each code configuration, giving it a consistent statistical meaning and avoiding per-channel calibration. DBN-SCF decoding selects candidate flip positions from the information set in the natural successive cancellation (SC) decoding order using a threshold, without sorting. Moreover, DBN-SCF decoding achieves better error-correction performance with a limited number of re-decoding attempts. It also requires lower average decoding complexity than existing SCF decoding methods at a comparable level of error-correction performance.

items.title: A high-order structure-preserving ALE--SAV finite element method for moving contact line flows
items.summary: We develop a structure-preserving arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) finite element method for incompressible Navier--Stokes flow with gravity and moving contact lines, based on a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) reformulation. The reformulation expresses the geometric energy quadratically in the auxiliary variable and permits linear treatment of the capillary, wetting and gravitational forces. The method combines high-order isoparametric elements in space with a linearly implicit, second-order Crank--Nicolson discretization in time. Second-order extrapolation supplies the predicted geometry and known coefficients of the linear fluid--SAV system. Mesh motion changes the kinetic-energy inner product and requires a compatible discretization of the time-derivative terms in the ALE formulation. We discretize these terms using an $L^2$-isometric velocity transfer to retain the kinetic-energy balance after the geometry update. We also construct a boundary update that preserves area or volume exactly using only linear solves. The resulting scheme satisfies a discrete SAV energy-dissipation law and preserves area or volume exactly. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions demonstrate high-order spatial and second-order temporal convergence and confirm SAV energy dissipation and area or volume conservation.

items.title: Quantum channel bounds for constant-composition codes
items.summary: We extend the quantum-channel optimization of Alrabiah and Guruswami to $q$-ary constant-composition codes. We study explicit channel and flag constructions that recover selected classical asymptotic upper bounds, including the Ben-Haim--Litsyn, moving-subspace and Horn-channel bounds. We give two equivalent formulations, Gram and flag, and prove stability of the obtained upper bounds under permutation transport and generalized shortening. A hierarchy defined by bounding the output-state ranks within each flag improves strictly between consecutive levels at every composition and every positive distance below the Plotkin threshold. We provide finite matrix parametrizations of these bounds (i.e., the number of variables does not depend on the length of codes under consideration). Numerical optimization rapidly produces improvements over the known asymptotic upper bounds throughout all tested nonbinary parameter ranges. For rational input data, each finite level admits near-optimal feasible rational descriptions of polynomial length. Their feasibility can be checked exactly and their objective values computed to any prescribed accuracy in polynomial time; the associated threshold problem with a prescribed gap belongs to $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$.

items.title: A Low-Rank Augmented Lagrangian Frank-Wolfe-Based Method for SDPs with Unbounded Feasible Regions
items.summary: In contrast to HALLaR (Monteiro et al. 2026), which is designed for solving problems with a trace-bounding constraint, this work develops a new augmented Lagrangian (AL) method, HALLaR+, for solving large-scale semidefinite programming problems without such constraint. Even though a trace constraint which preserves an optimal solution can always be added, choosing its bound is challenging: a value that is too small may exclude all optimal solutions, whereas one that is too large may substantially increase the computational effort. HALLaR+ is also a low-rank inexact AL method but, in contrast to HALLaR, it doubles the penalty parameter at every AL iteration and its AL subproblems have unbounded feasible regions that are approximately solved by a relaxed unbounded Frank--Wolfe (RUFW) variant. Its analysis relies on a uniform bound on the diameters of the sublevel sets of all generated AL subproblems instead of a bounded feasible set. Assuming that a primal--dual KKT pair exists and the primal optimal set is nonempty and bounded, it is shown that HALLaR+ returns a $\varepsilon$-primal-dual feasible solution in $\tilde {\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ total RUFW iterations. Numerical results suggest that HALLaR+ has very promising competitive performance against current state-of-the-art solvers.

items.title: Gradient Estimation for LLM-Embedded Simulation Optimization
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in operational simulators to represent context-dependent human decisions, which opens new possibilities for simulation optimization. However, the LLM acts as a black box, so derivatives through its decisions are unavailable for gradient-based policy search. Finite difference estimation can avoid this requirement, but the required paired simulations that sample LLM actions independently often disagree, and such action switches persist under small perturbations, which inflates the gradient variance to order $c^{-2}$ for perturbation radius $c$. To control this variance, we develop a behavioral common random number framework. It first applies maximal coupling to the LLM's action distributions, preserving each simulation's behavioral law while making action switches as rare as possible, which reduces the variance bound to $O(c^{-1})$. It then applies first-switch conditioning, which averages over whether a switch occurs, together with an impact-aware extension that prioritizes influential switches. Under suitable stability conditions, both keep the variance bounded as $c$ shrinks. We further establish improved complexity bounds for projected stochastic approximation. Experiments on synthesized and LLM-embedded simulators confirm the theory and show substantial performance gains.

items.title: Zeroth-Order Riemannian Optimization on Fixed-Rank Manifolds for LLM Fine-Tuning
items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

items.title: Integral Compensation for Discrete-time Bearing-only Target Localization and Circumnavigation
items.summary: This paper investigates the discrete-time control problem of driving an agent to localize and circumnavigate an unknown target at a prescribed radius using bearing measurements. Discretizing existing continuous-time circumnavigation controllers can introduce steady-state orbit bias, even at sampling rates that preserve stability. To eliminate the sampling-induced orbit bias, we propose an adaptive compensator for a circumnavigation controller formulated directly in discrete time. Driven by the estimated agent-to-target distance, the proposed compensator dynamically learns the geometric correction required to achieve the desired circumnavigation radius. Unlike existing static correction methods, neither the proposed controller nor the compensator update explicitly uses the sampling interval. Exponential convergence is rigorously established using Lyapunov-based analysis. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithms.

items.title: A Bayesian oriented exploration and reinforcement learning in continuous-time mean-variance portfolio optimization
items.summary: We propose a new reinforcement learning (RL) framework for the continuous-time mean-variance portfolio optimization with unknown market parameters. To better reflect the impact of improved information of the unknown drift on the degree of exploration, we consider a novel randomization based on continuous-time stochastic filtering. Specifically, we construct a continuous-time analog to Thompson Sampling by treating the unknown drift as a random draw from a generalized sampling distribution parameterized by the filter's posterior mean and variance. The new learning objective measures the tradeoff between the wealth performance and the weighted KL divergence between the policy and the true Bayesian posterior, which transforms the classical feedback control into an information guided stochastic policy. As a result, the degree of exploration endogenously depends on the Reward-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimation that decays with the shrinking filter's variance. This allows us to devise an efficient model-based learning algorithm in the mean-variance portfolio optimization with theoretical guarantee and superior learning performance.

items.title: Performance Analysis of Entanglement Swapping DV-QKD over MIMO FSO Channels
items.summary: This paper studies multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) free-space optical (FSO) quantum communication systems employing polarization-encoded discrete-variable quantum key distribution (DV-QKD), based on entanglement swapping, with the goal of extending secure communications beyond the reach of a direct link. The FSO channels are subject to atmospheric absorption, diffraction, beam wander, pointing errors, and turbulence-induced fading, while background noise and detector imperfections degrade the performance. An eavesdropper controlling the channels and the relay is also considered. To analyze the performance of the considered system, both hops MIMO channels are decomposed into parallel spatial eigenchannels via singular value decomposition (SVD), photon loss is modeled using Kraus operators, and a threshold-detector model is developed for the relay. Based on these models, closed-form per-eigenchannel expressions for the relay gain are derived, which are then used to obtain expressions for the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and the secret key rate (SKR). Numerical results demonstrate that entanglement swapping maintains a low QBER over longer distances than direct transmission, extending the communication range beyond the noise-limited cutoff of the direct link, at the cost of a lower SKR at short distances. The crossover distance beyond which entanglement swapping prevails is determined mainly by the background noise and the detector technology, and it is demonstrated to increase with MIMO configurations. Moreover, the reach gain is shown to be maximized for a midpoint relay. Finally, since each swapping event requires a single-pair emission from both sources, a near-deterministic entangled-photon source is required, which spontaneous parametric down-conversion sources do not provide at practical key rates, whereas MIMO substantially relaxes this requirement.

items.title: Weighted Matroid Intersection under Minimum Rank Oracle
items.summary: We consider matroid intersection under the minimum rank oracle model, in which two matroids are accessible only through an oracle that returns the minimum of the ranks of a given set in the two matroids. By Edmonds' theorem, this oracle determines the matroid intersection polytope, although it does not reveal the exchangeability graphs on which classical algorithms rely. Recent work by Bárász, Bérczi, Király, Oki, Yamaguchi, and Yokoi (2025) showed that unweighted matroid intersection is polynomially solvable in this model. In this paper, we present a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for weighted matroid intersection in this model. The key to our algorithm is a polynomial-size extended formulation of tangent cones of common base polytopes that can be constructed using the minimum rank oracle. We also give min-max theorems in terms of the minimum rank function via 1/3-submodularity, and present a strongly polynomial-time algorithm to compute an optimal dual solution.

items.title: Spectral Bias Reduction in Local Gated ReLU Architectures
items.summary: Neural networks trained by gradient-based methods learn the low-frequency content of a target function faster than its high-frequency content. This spectral bias is well documented, but it is much less clear which architectural choices mitigate it and which cannot. We study the question for shallow ReLU models linear in their trainable parameters, where each mode is learned at a rate given by a Gram-matrix eigenvalue, and for a general symmetric bilinear form $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, so that least-squares regression ($a=$ the $L^2$ inner product) and variational or physics-informed losses ($a=$ the $H^1$ energy form) are two instances of one analysis. Within this framework we propose gated local ReLU dictionaries, obtained by multiplying each ReLU feature by a hat partition-of-unity weight, in the spirit of partition-of-unity finite elements and overlapping Schwarz methods. The resulting Gram matrices are block-banded for any local bilinear form, with a block-Toeplitz interior whose matrix-valued symbol governs the spectrum. The two forms then behave very differently. For $L^2$ regression, the symbol is bounded away from zero, the ratio is uniform in the number of windows, and the measured spread of frequency-dependent learning rates falls from $1.9\times10^{5}$ to $4.5$ at matched model size. For the $H^1$ stiffness matrix, the symbol vanishes at zero frequency: gating leaves the $Θ(N^2)$ conditioning intact and inverts the frequency ordering instead of removing the bias. A preconditioner built from the same interior stencil will fix the spectral bias, showing that architecture alone is not enough. Experiments on $1$D regression and Poisson problems confirm the dichotomy, and the regression effect persists when the hidden-layer parameters are trained as well.

items.title: Port-Hamiltonian Systems Beyond Joules: A Review of Unexpected Application Domains
items.summary: The port-Hamiltonian framework was built for mechanical and electrical systems, where the Hamiltonian is stored energy and the ports carry power. Over the past fifteen years it has spread to chemistry, cell biology, fusion plasmas, musical instruments, district heating, electricity markets, macroeconomics, predator-prey ecology, optimization algorithms and neural-network training. This review maps that spread. We classify each application by what its Hamiltonian really is: physical energy, a thermodynamic potential such as free energy or exergy, or an abstract storage function with no energetic meaning. The review keeps only sources whose bibliographic record we checked against Crossref. The picture that emerges is a continuum. Where a genuine thermodynamic potential exists, the theory is deep and constructive. Where the energy is borrowed, the framework still pays off through compositional interconnection and dissipation inequalities, but the work is younger and scattered. We close with a set of deliberately speculative research directions, including open port-Hamiltonian models of epidemics, opinion dynamics and supply chains, and learned port-Hamiltonian digital twins for structural health monitoring.

items.title: An Improved Algorithm for Quantified Boolean Formulas
items.summary: Quantified Boolean formula (QBF), the quantified version of Boolean satisfiability (SAT), is a fundamental problem in constraint solving. Due to the $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete nature of QBF, designing theoretically efficient QBF algorithms is much harder and receives less attention in academia. In this work, we present a new algorithm based on memoized search, which solves QBF with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses in $1.685^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ time and space. This is the first improvement over the $1.709^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ bound by Williams in over 20 years. Our technique is based on the minimum vertex cover of the conflict graphs, which was proposed to study the parameterized complexity of SAT. We extend this idea to QBF and further show that QBF is slicewise polynomial-time solvable using this parameter.

items.title: Strong relaxed dynamics in stochastic control
items.summary: We characterize relaxed dynamics for which any finite family of strong state solutions, together with their relaxed inputs, can be approximated by the prescribed controlled dynamics, ground-stably in law. Relaxed inputs include parametrizations of relaxed controls over the unit interval. Unlike relaxed controls, these parametrizations determine action couplings. The proposed relaxed dynamics is driven by a single cylindrical Brownian motion in a Hilbert space. For each relaxed input, its state is the unique strong solution of the corresponding equation. The collection of these states, over all relaxed inputs, satisfies the approximation requirement. Conversely, suppose one assigns to each relaxed input a continuous adapted state process on a fixed probability space. Pairwise approximation forces the assignment to be the strong solution map of the same dynamics, for a unique cylindrical Brownian driver. In fact, even for a state map indexed by (non-parametrized) relaxed controls, the relevant relaxed control class admits coherent parametrizations under separability and finite-family approximation assumptions, and the same type of dynamics is recovered again.

items.title: Learning-Assisted Beamforming Optimization for Hybrid XL-RIS-Aided Communication
items.summary: Hybrid active-passive extremely large-scale reconfigurable intelligent surface (XL-RIS) architectures mitigate the double-hop path loss of passive RIS while enabling near-field spatial energy focusing, but impose a computationally intensive mixed discrete-continuous beamforming design problem under strict radio-frequency (RF) power constraints. This paper investigates a hybrid XL-RIS-assisted downlink multi-user multiple-input single-output (MU-MISO) system in the near-field regime. The joint optimization of the base station (BS) precoder, discrete XL-RIS phase shifts, and active-element amplification gains is addressed via a discrete coordinate ascent (DCA)-based alternating optimization (AO) framework, in which discrete variables are updated through local index-domain searches and the BS precoder is derived in closed form via a noise-aware minimum mean-square error (MMSE) criterion. To reduce the per-sample computational cost for XL-RIS apertures, a deep unfolding (DU) framework is proposed as a low-complexity alternative, unrolling a fixed number of Riemannian gradient ascent steps on the sum-rate objective and recovering the discrete phase configuration via quantized phasor projection, with one learnable step size per layer trained in a self-supervised manner. Numerical results under near-field spherical-wave channel models confirm that the DU framework achieves sum-rate performance close to the AO scheme with substantially lower and nearly constant runtime, and that both schemes consistently outperform manifold optimization under discrete hardware constraints.

items.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
items.summary: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $δ$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $δ$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.

items.title: Error Estimates and Convergence Analysis for Learning Mechanism--AI Coupled Dynamical Systems
items.summary: Mechanism--AI coupled dynamical systems retain known mechanisms while learning unknown dynamics from data. We study how neural approximation, numerical integration, finite observations, and optimization jointly affect the accuracy of this learning process. For time-dependent learned terms in a fixed compact admissible class, we derive a four-component objective error bound within an optimal control formulation. Explicit estimates are obtained for constrained ReLU approximation and Euler integration, with deterministic quadrature and random sampling treated separately. Under joint refinement, we establish $Γ$-convergence of the approximate objectives and show that approximate minimizers approach the continuous optimal set when the global optimization gaps vanish. We also derive conditional stability estimates for state-dependent learned terms. Numerical experiments with a susceptible--infected--recovered (SIR) model illustrate the analysis and show how solver resolution affects continuous-trajectory accuracy even when training losses are similar.

items.title: Reconstructing Interacting Blood Flow and Wall Interface Deformation from Noisy Flow Data Using PirateNets
items.summary: Blood flow and elastic vessel-wall motion interact with each other: fluid stress drives wall deformation, while the moving wall changes the domain in which blood flows. Given noisy flow images, we study the inverse problem of reconstructing the coupled, unsteady three-dimensional motions. We solve the reconstruction through Gauss--Seidel-type alternating fluid and geometry updates. For the fluid, we use physics-informed networks to recover velocity and pressure by fitting the observations while enforcing the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on the moving domain, which is described by an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) map. For the geometry, a reference-domain correction and sequential registration recover the vessel shape and wall displacement. Interface traction continuity and an elastic momentum equation regularize the registration so that the recovered displacement is also physics-informed. The networks evaluate fields and physical residuals at sampled space--time points without remeshing the moving domain. Experiments on a converging channel and a patient-like aorta demonstrate reconstruction of flow and wall motion from noisy data. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies examine the role of structure regularization and imperfect physical coefficients. A further experiment with a three-element Windkessel outlet condition demonstrates how the framework accommodates a more physiologically realistic boundary setting.

items.title: Geometric Stochastic Dynamics and Fokker-Planck Equation on $\mathsf{T}\mathbb S^2$
items.summary: This paper develops a geometric (coordinate-free) stochastic model of a controlled point mass evolving on the unit two-sphere $\mathbb S^2$, together with the Fokker-Planck equation governing the probability density of the resulting stochastic process. The state manifold is the tangent bundle $\mathsf{T}\mathbb S^2$. The Levi-Civita connection of the round metric is used to construct the horizontal-vertical splitting of $\mathsf{T}(\mathsf{T}\mathbb S^2)$ and to convert the intrinsic second-order dynamics of the system into a first-order controlled vector field on $\mathsf{T}\mathbb S^2$. Endowing the tangent bundle with the Sasaki metric then permits stochastic perturbations to be introduced intrinsically and independently in horizontal, i.e., position, and vertical, i.e., velocity, directions. The corresponding infinitesimal generator is obtained in horizontal-vertical Hessian form. The probability density is defined with respect to the Sasaki Riemannian volume measure. The Fokker-Planck equation is derived intrinsically in both Stratonovich and Itô forms. In the Itô representation, a globally defined horizontal-vertical diffusion tensor yields a compact double-divergence Fokker-Planck PDE. No coordinates or embedded Euclidean representation of the sphere dynamics are used in the development. Numerical simulations illustrate the stochastic motion of a controlled particle ensemble on $\mathbb S^2$ toward an antipodal target configuration.

items.title: A Trajectory-Aware Domain-Decomposed Multispace Reduced Basis Preconditioner for Parametric Helmholtz Problems
items.summary: Repeated solutions of parametric Helmholtz problems arise in multi-query applications such as sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. Classical preconditioned iterative solvers do not automatically reuse low-dimensional structures across parameters. Multispace reduced basis (MSRB) preconditioners can exploit such structures by constructing iteration-specific reduced order models (ROMs) from training data, but storing global iteration-dependent bases incurs substantial memory costs. Building on trajectory-aware MSRB training, we develop a domain-decomposed MSRB (DD-MSRB) preconditioner for parametric Helmholtz systems truncated by perfectly matched layers (PMLs). Within flexible GMRES, each reduced space is trained on inverse-action snapshots along the Krylov trajectories generated by the ROM-based preconditioners applied in preceding iterations. To reduce storage, problem-adapted spatial partitions exploit heterogeneous local snapshot compressibility across the physical interior and the PML. Local basis dimensions in each subdomain are determined greedily under a global snapshot-error budget to balance approximation accuracy and storage. The resulting hybrid solver applies DD-MSRB preconditioning during the initial iterations to capture dominant cross-parameter modes and then switches, when necessary, to a shifted-Laplacian preconditioner to reduce error components poorly represented by the reduced spaces. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional half-space propagation, elliptic-obstacle scattering, and three-dimensional waveguides demonstrate significant acceleration over the shifted-Laplacian baseline and substantial memory savings relative to global MSRB. For the largest waveguide system, with 11.0 million unknowns, DD-MSRB reduces deployed ROM storage by 44.9% and mean online solve time by 30.2% compared with global MSRB.

items.title: GEAR: A GPU-Accelerated Global Solver for Bounded Continuous Nonlinear Programs via Linear Bound Propagation
items.summary: We present a novel GPU-accelerated global solver for constrained nonlinear programming (NLP) inspired by the efficient linear bound propagation framework in neural network (NN) verification. Existing work on NN verification, a problem that can be cast as feasibility detection for a nonlinear objective, demonstrated orders-of-magnitude speedups with the linear bound propagation-based framework when compared to traditional solvers. Extending this paradigm to global nonlinear programming requires addressing many challenges: a global constrained NLP solver must effectively exploit all, possibly unstructured, nonlinear constraints to improve the objective, whereas NN verification typically handles simple input box constraints over a well-structured NN and does not directly optimize an objective function. We address these challenges by fully exploiting the linear bounds produced by bound propagation: these linear bounds can be viewed as relaxations of nonlinear constraints and used to provide lower bounds, check infeasibility, and guide the search for a primal solution. In addition, we propose tighter linear relaxations for bilinear, quotient, and other commonly used nonlinear functions in NLP problems, and a projected augmented Lagrangian method tightly coupled to our dual solving procedure to produce primal solutions. Our method solves 421 of 505 bounded and continuous NLP problems in the GAMS and MINLPLib benchmarks under a 180-second limit, more than each of the six global solvers we compare with, including Gurobi and BARON (commercial), and SCIP (open-source). Sixteen of these problems are certified by none of the six global solvers; all of them contain exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric terms, which are often challenging for traditional approaches. Project webpage is at https://verified-intelligence.github.io/GEAR.

items.title: Zeroth-Order Langevin Dynamics for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization: Curvature Regularization and Non-Asymptotic Guarantees
items.summary: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies the objective being optimized. In particular, Gaussian smoothing with smoothing parameter $η>0$ induces, to leading order, an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, which motivates the study of the curvature-regularized objective of the form $f(x)+(η^2/2) tr(\nabla^2 f(x))$. We develop a non-asymptotic theory in the nonconvex setting for a class of algorithms called stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD), which use only noisy function evaluations and do not have access to first- or higher-order derivative information, and derive excess-risk guarantees for the curvature-regularized objective. We first control the finite-time distribution of the ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance with respect to the Gibbs measure associated with the Gaussian-smoothed objective. An explicit coupling between the smoothing and inverse temperature parameters then quantifies the proximity of this measure to the Gibbs measure associated with the corresponding Hessian-trace-regularized objective. These distributional estimates in Wasserstein distance lead to excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective. Our analysis accommodates assumptions under which the stochastic function evaluations are allowed to have non-uniform dependence on the data stream. In addition, the constants in the non-asymptotic bounds do not rely on log-Sobolev or Poincaré inequalities as in prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that simultaneously establishes excess-risk guarantees for a curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure in the nonconvex setting.

items.title: High-order long-time stable methods for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations
items.summary: We present in this paper two scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) correction steps for constructing long-time stable schemes for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. A main feature is that the same correction steps apply to any linear predictor satisfying the order and spatial regularity requirements in Assumption~P. Their construction and stability analysis are independent of the particular form of the predictor and require no energy estimate for it. The first correction uses a damped, shifted kinetic-energy variable to obtain a uniform-in-time $L^2$ bound in two and three dimensions, together with a weighted dissipation estimate. In two dimensions, the second correction combines a higher-energy auxiliary variable with a scalar relaxation to yield a uniform-in-time $H^1$ bound. Under the stated assumptions, these estimates hold on arbitrary positive time grids, without restrictions on step sizes or adjacent step ratios. We also derive eventual absorbing bounds; for the two-SAV scheme, these apply to the admissible initial class associated with fixed parameters. The generalized BDF schemes require one constant-coefficient Helmholtz solve per velocity component and one pressure Poisson solve per step; the second correction adds no field solve. Numerical experiments exhibit second-, third-, and fourth-order convergence for the tested BDF schemes and illustrate the long-time stability and efficiency of adaptive time stepping.

items.title: Basis selection, universal sampling discretization, and sampling recovery
items.summary: For every real $N$-dimensional subspace of $L_2$, we construct one orthonormal basis such that, for every $1\le v\le N$, at most $Cv\log(eN/v)$ positively weighted samples discretize the squared $L_2$ norm of all $v$-term combinations. Random rotations also give simultaneous weighted $L_p$ estimates and a sharp $C\log(eN)$ bound for the squared $L_2$ norm of the pointwise maximum. For prescribed coefficient classes, a change of measure yields sampling recovery estimates from $Cv\log^3(2v)$ samples under a lower Riesz inequality and a common square-integrable pointwise bound.

items.title: Discrete-Time Zero-Sum Markov Games with Control, Stopping, and State-Dependent Discounting
items.summary: We study a discrete-time two-player zero-sum stochastic game with control and stopping, where both players can stop the game, the discount factors depends on the states, and the running and terminal rewards may be unbounded. A contraction argument for the constrained Shapley equation establishes the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium consisting of stationary controls and stopping times. We further provides algorithms for approximating the value and computing an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium. A numerical example with state-dependent discount factors illustrates the results.

items.title: How good are spline spaces for the Kolmogorov $n$-width of a Sobolev ball?
items.summary: This paper studies the approximation power of polynomial splines on a uniform one-dimensional mesh. The quality of the best approximation of the unit ball of $H^{s}$ by an $n$-dimensional subspace, measured in the $L^{2}$ norm, is quantified by the sup-inf of that space: for each function in the Sobolev ball, take its minimal approximation error over the space, and then take the supremum of these errors over the ball. The infimum of this sup-inf over all $n$-dimensional spaces is the well-known Kolmogorov $n$-width $d_{n}$. Choosing the $n$-dimensional subspace to be the piecewise polynomial space of degree $k$ with smoothness $C^μ$ ($-1\leμ\le k-1$) gives our sup-inf $E$. The approximation accuracy of spline spaces is then examined by comparing $d_{n}$ and $E$. The two quantities are determined by two eigenvalue problems, through which we obtain a lower bound for $d_{n}$ and an upper bound for $E$. Under the restriction $k\ge s-1$, the upper bound for the error of the maximally smooth spline space ($μ=k-1$) is asymptotically equal to the lower bound for $d_n$, showing that uniform $B$-splines are asymptotically optimal among all $n$-dimensional spaces. For $μ<k-1$, we prove that $E/d_n$ is bounded below by a constant strictly larger than $1$, except when $k>s-1$ and $μ=k-2$ hold simultaneously. This reveals the superiority of $B$-splines in the sense of $n$-widths. Numerical experiments corroborate these bounds and, in some cases (e.g. the exception above), show that they are sharp.

items.title: Simulating Nonlinear Resistive Networks using a Behavioral Splitting
items.summary: An operator splitting method is developed for computing operating points of nonlinear resistive networks. Our behavioral formulation separates the device laws from Kirchhoff's laws and casts simulation as a zero-finding problem. Branch port resistances then provide a diagonal preconditioner for the relaxed Peaceman-Rachford iteration in scattering variables. Each iteration requires solving independent scalar equations and a linear system with a fixed weighted Laplacian matrix. Convergence is established for maximal monotone device laws when an operating point exists. Contractive branch reflections also yield a linear convergence bound independent of network topology. Numerical experiments on crossbar arrays illustrate the computational advantages.

items.title: Sample complexity and scalability of adaptive-sampling trust-region methods for zeroth-order stochastic optimization --- Part I: common random numbers meet supermartingales
items.summary: We analyze adaptive sampling stochastic model-based trust-region methods that build their models in random subspaces and use common random numbers (CRN) within an iteration, and obtain, within a STORM-type analysis, the first $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ bound on the number of function evaluations needed to reach $\varepsilon$-stationarity, both almost surely and in expectation. The subspace model reduces the per-iteration computational cost, which allows scalability. The analysis relies on a general framework for the complexity of adaptive stochastic processes that carries the almost-sure analysis of ASTRO-DF into the STORM setting and adds expected bounds by a direct counting argument, without the renewal-reward argument of Blanchet et al. (2019). The bounds are obtained for two variants of a stochastic model-based trust-region method that differ in how the function evaluations used to measure progress are generated. The first algorithm, ASTRA-F, proceeds in a STORM-like manner: the trial point and the incumbent are re-evaluated on an independent set of replications, so that the estimates entering the acceptance test are independent of the model, as every existing STORM-type analysis requires their accuracy to be assessed conditionally on the model. The second, ASTRA-R, allows a practical approach: the trial point is evaluated on the replications already drawn to build the model, which avoids re-evaluating the incumbent, needs one adaptive sample size per iteration instead of two, and reduces the randomness entering the iteration. To our knowledge, no STORM-type analysis has been able to accommodate the latter approach as the accuracy of an estimate at a point chosen from the samples cannot be assessed conditionally on the model; we overcome this with a probabilistic chaining argument.

items.title: Sparse Predict and Demote: Optimal Scheduling with Minimal Size Advice
items.summary: Knowledge of job sizes is crucial for optimizing the mean response time in single-server scheduling. However, predictions of job sizes are typically inexact and may be costly to obtain. Thus, a long-standing research question is: what is the minimal information about job sizes required to obtain near-optimal mean response time? We introduce a novel policy, \emph{Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD)}, and prove that it achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic while requiring only one-bit job-size predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals. SPD achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality even in situations when predictions are (i) inexact up to any fixed multiplicative error bound, and (ii) costly, i.e., the server is used to compute predictions and is thus unavailable to serve jobs while processing prediction queries. Finally, we use numerical experiments to illustrate that SPD maintains near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.

items.title: Costate-Conditioned Dynamic Programming for Parallel-in-Time Solution of Equality-Constrained Optimal Control Problems
items.summary: When interior-point methods are applied to solve numerical trajectory optimisation problems, they spend most of their per-iteration time on a structured Newton--KKT system, associated to an equality-constrained linear-quadratic optimal control problem. Riccati-type algorithms exhibit linear complexity in the trajectory horizon. Parallel-in-time algorithms are able to reduce this to logaritmic complexity by distributing several subtrajectories over multiple cores and then stitch together the results by means of an associative scan. Existing exact formulations condition each subtrajectory on its terminal state. Each subproblem then carries the reachability to that terminal state explicitly as constraint rows. The associated reachability decision however is ill-conditioned for weakly actuated systems. In this work we condition each subtrajectory on the terminal costate instead. The resulting subproblems can now be computed by a free-end Riccati recursion without reachability carrying rows. This approach effectively compensates for the ill-conditioning of weakly actuated systems but requires additional bookkeeping with Lagrangian multipliers when stitching together the various subproblems. Numerically the method reproduces a direct solution of the primal-dual Newton-KKT system to $10^{-12}$ in relative terms, on a weakly controllable chain of masses, the accurracy rivals that of a sequential recursion, whereas terminal-state conditioning loses up to six digits or fails. Operation counts on a problem with 64 subtrajectories and a horizon of 4096 stages gives a speed-up of 26 compared with a sequential solve.

items.title: Memoryless BFGS on a nonsmooth convex function: two new results
items.summary: We extend the analysis of Asl and Overton~\cite{AO2021} for memoryless BFGS (also known as L-BFGS-1) using an Armijo-Wolfe line search and applied to the nonsmooth convex function $f(x)=a|x^{(1)}|+\sum_{i=2}^n x^{(i)}$, where $n\ge2$ and $a \geq \sqrt{n-1}$. This function is unbounded below, so the method is successful if it generates function values diverging to $-\infty$, and fails otherwise. For scaled L-BFGS-1, we sharpen the sufficient condition for % az{convergence of the absolute normalized search directions} in Theorem~3.1 of failure in \cite{AO2021} from $a\ge2\sqrt{n-1}$ to $a\ge\sqrt{3(n-1)}$. For the unscaled version, we prove success for every $a$: either the method generates a direction along which no Armijo-Wolfe step exists, certifying unboundedness below, or its function values diverge to $-\infty$. Both results are consistent with the numerical experiments in \cite{AO2021}. Both proofs given here were derived with help from GPT 6 in discussions directed by the first author and corrected and rephrased afterward.

items.title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
items.summary: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{é}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.

items.title: Convergence of Adaptive Least Squares Finite Element Methods
items.summary: We consider a general class of operator equations $\mathcal B u=f$ where $\mathcal B:\mathbb U\to \mathbb L_2$ is a linear isomorphis from a Hilbert space $\mathbb U$ onto an ``$L_2$-type'' space $\mathbb L_2 = L_2(Ω;\mathbb R^q)$. This covers weak first order formulations of stationary elliptic boundary value problems, the Stokes system or systems for linear elasticity as well as space-time formulations of heat or wave equations. Since an $L_2$-residual is uniformly equivalent to the corresponding error in the trial space norm reliable and efficient computable a posteriori error bounds are for free. In contrast to a matured theory of classical adaptive finite element methods, estblishing linear convergence - and eventually optimal complexity - in a least squares setting seems to have remained open. To a large extent this is due to the fact that least squares error indicators do not exhibit any explicit dependence on local mesh-sizes. In this paper we propose a rather different approach to establish under which circumstances standard Dörfler-marking mesh refinement gives rise to linear convergence and rate optimality of adaptive least squares finite element methods as well. A central role is played by a new notion of {\em data-visibility} which is a structural property of the data rather than a smoothness condition.

items.title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions
items.summary: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which Göloğlu and Pavlů proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certificates. No function in these classes or in their switching closure is CCZ-equivalent to a permutation. All code and data are public.

items.title: Transport Less, Solve Faster: Exploiting sparsity in algorithm design for Unbalanced Optimal Transport
items.summary: In this paper, we study the computational aspects of the Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem between two given positive measures $μ$ and $ν$. The UOT is a variant to the classic Optimal Transportation problem in which the linear constraints modeling mass preservation are relaxed and replaced by a convex penalty $\Dphi$ in the objective function. First, we show that any UOT problem admits a discrete solution as long as $μ$ and $ν$ are discrete, allowing us to express the optimality conditions characterizing the solution to the UOT problem in an easy-to-handle form. By exploiting the optimality conditions we provide an upper and lower bound on the marginals of the solution as well as a bound on the mass that any solution assigns to any couple of points. The bounds on the mass assigned to each couple of points reveal that, under suitable conditions, the support of any solution to the UOT is contained within a compact set that does not depend on the measures $μ$ and $ν$, but only on the penalty function $\Dphi$ and the cost function $c$. We then introduce a truncated version of the UOT problem that fully leverages the sparsity of the optimal solution by introducing a parameter $R$ that saturates $c$. We show that any solution to the truncated problem naturally yields an approximation of the optimal solution for the standard UOT problem and bound the primal sub-optimality gap between the real solution and the solution induced by the truncated problem via a decreasing power-like function of $R$. Lastly, we study the convergence speed of the Pairwise Frank-Wolfe algorithm when applied to the truncated UOT problem and show that such routine is able to identify the support of the solution within a finite number of iterations.

items.title: Lower-Level Agnostic Bilevel Optimization
items.summary: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel algorithms typically assume that the LL objective is available for evaluation, differentiation, or unrolling. However, this assumption can fail when the LL response is produced by a black-box solver, simulator, adversary, or learned predictor. In this paper, we study LL agnostic bilevel optimization, where the UL learner has access only to an approximate LL solution $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ and cannot query the LL objective, its gradients, Hessian/Jacobian information, or the procedure that generates the LL response. We propose LeGo-BiO, a coordinate-wise pseudo-hypergradient method that estimates the missing Jacobian $\nabla _{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ using finite differences of $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\cdot)$. For each UL coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector subject to 1-sparse updates, thereby isolating the corresponding Jacobian column needed in the UL gradient computation. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and, unlike derivative-free/zeroth-order approximations of the entire UL gradient, preserves the available first-order gradient information with respect to the UL variables for more accurate UL gradient evaluation. We establish convergence guarantees for LeGo-BiO in both deterministic and stochastic settings under an LL error-bound/Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition, without requiring LL strong convexity. Our bounds yield an $O(T^{-1})$ rate in the deterministic setting and an $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate in the stochastic setting when the LL approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments demonstrate competitive performance of LeGo-BiO despite being agnostic to the LL objective.

items.title: Randomized Greedy MIS Is Fast at Every Node of a Tree
items.summary: The Randomized Greedy MIS (RGMIS) algorithm computes a maximal independent set (MIS) by processing the vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily adding each vertex to the independent set whenever possible. Despite its simplicity, this algorithm has proved effective in a range of parallel, distributed, and dynamic settings. For sufficiently small maximum degree, Nguyen and Onak (FOCS~'08) and Yoshida, Yamamoto, and Ito (STOC~'09) showed that a recursive simulation of RGMIS can be used to estimate the sizes of matching and vertex cover in sublinear time. The key subroutine in their approach is the following local query procedure: given a vertex $v$, to determine whether $v$ belongs to the MIS, recursively evaluate the neighbors of $v$ that precede $v$ in the random order. If any such neighbor is found to belong to the MIS, the procedure immediately concludes that $v$ is not in the MIS; otherwise, it concludes that $v$ is in the MIS. For graphs of maximum degree $Δ$, Nguyen and Onak showed that, in expectation over the random ordering, this procedure makes $O(\exp(Δ))$ recursive calls from a worst-case starting vertex. No better upper bound is known even for trees. We prove that on trees, from \textit{any} starting vertex, this recursive RGMIS procedure makes $\mathrm{poly}(Δ)$ recursive calls in expectation.

items.title: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee
items.summary: In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator (DisMUSE), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, DisMUSE integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an $O((KT)^{-1/3})$ convergence rate, where $K$ and $T$ denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our DisMUSE method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost.

items.title: Laplace approximation of the parameter posterior with embedded error for efficient uncertainty quantification of expensive model calibrations
items.summary: In practical engineering, there is a clear need for uncertainty quantification (UQ) of models used in design because forward UQ puts probabilities on performance predictions. However, without surrogate building, most forward engineering models are too expensive for traditional UQ methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our goal is to provide inexpensive, approxi- mate UQ that can be applied after an expensive traditional least squares fit, where the UQ handles both uncorrelated noise and parameter variance as in the embedded-error treatment developed by Sargsyan, Najm, and Ghanem (2015). After developing the basic theory to connect a Laplace-like approximation to Bayesian calibration, we compare the proposed method to black-box variational inference in terms of cost and fidelity. Then we demonstrate the method on real-world calibration of solid material models.

items.title: Linear Convergence of Nesterov's Acceleration for All Momentum Parameter
items.summary: We study the convergence rate of the Nesetrov's accelerated proximal gradient method for a smooth, strongly convex composite minimization objective across a range of value of the momentum extrapolation. The literature proves a convergence rate of the method for a specific momentum extrapolation parameter choice based on the knowledge of strong convexity and Lipschitz smoothness constants. For the heavy ball method it is established that every choice of the momentum parameter either fails to accelerate or fails to converge on the same function class. We prove in this paper that a range of Nesterov style constant momentum extrapolation parameters produces a linear convergence rate. We corroborate these results numerically via performance estimation which computes a method's exact worst case rate as a semidefinite program.

items.title: Strong Connectivity Oracle for Multiple Failures via Rooted Flow-Augmentation
items.summary: We present a significantly improved $k$-fault-tolerant strong connectivity oracle, one of the most basic data structures on a directed graph $G$ that, given any set $F$ of failed edges of size $|F|\le k$, answers whether $G \setminus F$ is strongly connected. For every constant $k$, our oracle only uses $n^{1+o(1)}$ space and $n^{o(1)}$ query time. No prior result can achieve $o(n^{2})$ space and $o(n)$ query time, \emph{even when $k=2$}. Previous oracles either require $Ω(n)$ query time [BCR18], or $Ω(n^2)$ space [vdBS19]. Our main technical contribution is a \emph{rooted} version of the highly successful flow augmentation technique, which may be of independent interest. Given a directed graph $G$, an integer $k$, and a source vertex $s$, we can sample a set of edges $A$ such that each minimal $s$-rooted cut of size at most $k$ becomes an $s$-rooted min-cut in $G + A$ with probability $2^{-poly(k)}n^{-o(1)}$.

items.title: Flexible Edge Cover: A Disjunctive Programming driven Approximation
items.summary: We introduce the flexible edge cover problem, denoted FLEX-EDGE-COVER: the input here is an undirected graph with non-negative edge costs along with a partition of the edges into safe and unsafe edges, non-negative integers $p$ and $q$, and the goal is to find a minimum cost subset of edges such that each vertex has either at least $p$ safe edges incident to it or at least $p+q$ total edges incident to it. We show that FLEX-EDGE-COVER is APX-hard in simple bipartite graphs. A greedy approach leads to a $2$-approximation in all graphs. We show that the $2$-factor can be improved in simple graphs via a novel disjunctive programming-based LP formulation. AI-tools were used in the analysis of our rounding algorithm. Our motivation for introducing and investigating FLEX-EDGE-COVER is its close connection to the Flexible Graph Connectivity problem (denoted $(p,q)$-FGC) which has garnered much recent attention. For $(p,q)$-FGC, we develop a tighter LP-formulation via the disjunctive programming approach. We hope that our disjunctive-programming based LP and rounding algorithms for FLEX-EDGE-COVER will serve as a starting point towards a constant factor approximation for $(p,q)$-FGC.

items.title: BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach
items.summary: Stochastic bilevel optimization provides a general framework for many machine learning applications, such as hyperparameter learning, data reweighting, language model alignment, and actor-critic reinforcement learning. However, most existing bilevel optimization methods treat matrix-valued gradients as flattened vectors and perform optimization in the resulting vectorized space, ignoring the matrix structures common in modern neural networks. Moreover, the lower-level (LL) problem curvature can induce significant spectral imbalance in the upper-level (UL) geometry. Such limitations of existing bilevel optimization methods motivate us to develop BiMuon, a geometry-aware stochastic bilevel optimization method that integrates implicit hypergradient estimation in bilevel optimization with Muon-style orthogonalized updates at the UL. To our knowledge, BiMuon is the first stochastic BLO method with Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates and an $O(ε^{-4})$ iteration-complexity guarantee, matching the best-known rates achieved by Muon-type methods based on matrix parameterizations. To improve computational and parallel efficiency for models with multiple matrix parameters, we further study BiMuon for blockwise diagonal matrix approximation and derive a relative stepsize allocation rule based on UL progress and blockwise LL sensitivity. We evaluate BiMuon on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization, providing empirical support for our methods.

items.title: Fully Dynamic Correlation Clustering with Vertex Updates in Polylogarithmic Update Time
items.summary: We present a fully dynamic algorithm for correlation clustering that supports \emph{vertex} insertions and deletions while maintaining an $O(1)$ approximation in polylogarithmic amortized update time. This resolves an open problem of vertex deletions posed by a recent line of work on dynamic correlation clustering. We adopt the min-disagreement objective for correlation clustering, i.e., given a signed complete graph $G=(V,E^+\cup E^-)$, we want to minimize the total number of $(+)$ edge crossing clusters and $(-)$ edges within clusters. The input is given in the adjacency list model, where each update inserts or deletes a node along with its full set of $(+)$ neighbors. Our main technical contribution is a fault-tolerant sparse-dense decomposition framework which unlike the existing decomposition-based frameworks allows for structural inconsistencies as long as the induced cost is bounded. We also show a separation between explicitly maintaining the (stronger) sparse-dense decomposition and maintaining a constant-factor approximation to correlation clustering, which may be of independent interest.

items.title: A Note on the Hardness of Partially Dynamic Max Flow
items.summary: We study the fine-grained complexity of partially dynamic max flow in capacitated graphs. Assuming the combinatorial 4-clique hypothesis, combinatorial algorithms require $Ω(n^{2-o(1)})$ amortized update time. Thus, recomputing max flow after each update is optimal up to subpolynomial factors for combinatorial algorithms in dense graphs. The previous conditional lower bound was $Ω(n^{1-o(1)})$ amortized update time under SETH or the OMv hypothesis and applies to all algorithms [Dah16].

items.title: A Hierarchical Variational Inequality Approach to Generalized Nash Equilibrium Seeking with Nonlinear Shared Constraints
items.summary: We study the computation of variational generalized Nash equilibria (v-GNE) in games with strongly monotone pseudo-gradients and nonlinear convex shared constraints. We show that the v-GNE problem is exactly equivalent to a hierarchical variational inequality, whose lower level is given by the gradient of a smooth convex penalty of the constraint violation over the local action sets. Building on this reformulation, we propose a hierarchical regularization scheme that operates entirely in the primal space and requires only projections onto the local action sets. In the centralized setting, we prove last-iterate squared distance convergence to the v-GNE with rate $O(1/t^{\scriptscriptstyle 2/3})$ under a local error bound condition, which holds, e.g., under Slater's condition, improved to $O(1/t)$ under a global error bound condition. We then extend the scheme to the partial-decision information setting, where the agents communicate over a network and maintain local estimates of the joint action. We derive a distributed algorithm with a constant stepsize operating in the primal space and converging to the v-GNE with rate $O(1/t)$.

items.title: Dynamic Edge Orientation on Low-Arboricity Graphs: Breaking the $\log n$ Barrier
